objectives.summary: Privileged Identity Management (PIM) gives just-in-time, time-bound and approval-based access to Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resource roles and groups (PIM for Groups). Instead of standing (active) admin rights, users get eligible assignments they must activate, optionally with MFA, justification, ticket number, approval or a Conditional Access authentication context. Role settings (PIM policies) are defined per role, and exam questions often test their limits, default approvers and licensing.

keyFacts.fact: Activation maximum duration in PIM role settings can be set from 1 to 24 hours.

If 'Require approval to activate' is on but no approvers are selected, active Privileged Role Administrators and Global Administrators become the default approvers. Approvers don't need any role themselves.

You need at least the Privileged Role Administrator role to manage PIM role settings for a Microsoft Entra role. Settings apply per role, so every assignment of the same role shares the same settings.

PIM needs Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance licenses for users with eligible or time-bound assignments, for approvers, and for access reviewers. If the license expires, eligible Entra role assignments are removed, but permanent assignments stay.

Eligible Azure role assignments can be created for users but not for service principals or managed identities, because they can't perform activation. On Access control (IAM), eligible assignments are supported at management group, subscription and resource group scope, but not at resource scope.

If you require a Conditional Access authentication context on activation, don't scope that CA policy to the directory role itself. During activation the user doesn't hold the role yet, so the policy wouldn't apply. Scope it to all users or to the eligible users.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Entra admin center > ID Governance > Privileged Identity Management > Microsoft Entra roles > Roles > (select role) > Role settings > Edit

lab.title: Make a user eligible for Security Reader with MFA and approval
steps: In a trial tenant with Microsoft Entra ID P2 (or a P2 trial), sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as a Privileged Role Administrator.
Create a test user, User1, and a second user, Approver1.
Go to ID Governance > Privileged Identity Management > Microsoft Entra roles > Roles and select Security Reader.
Select Role settings > Edit. Set Activation maximum duration to 2 hours, select 'On activation, require multifactor authentication' and 'Require justification on activation'.
Select 'Require approval to activate' and add Approver1 as the approver. Select Update.
Go to Assignments > Add assignments, select Security Reader, choose User1, set Assignment type to Eligible and finish the wizard.
Sign in as User1 in a private browser window, open PIM > My roles > Eligible assignments and select Activate. Enter a justification and submit.
Sign in as Approver1, open PIM > Approve requests and approve the request.
lab.verify: As User1, PIM > My roles > Active assignments shows Security Reader with an end time no more than 2 hours away. The Microsoft Entra audit log shows the activation request and approval.

Admin1 creates a CA policy that targets c1 and the Security Administrator directory role and requires a compliant device. Admin1 then configures c1 in the PIM role settings. Eligible users find that they can still activate the role from non-compliant devices.
questions.question: What should Admin1 change?
options: Scope the CA policy to all users or to the eligible users, not to the Security Administrator directory role
Turn on 'On activation, require multifactor authentication' in addition to the authentication context
Set the CA policy to report-only mode so PIM's backup MFA protection applies
Reduce the activation maximum duration to 1 hour

A report-only policy never enforces controls, and the backup MFA mechanism isn't triggered for report-only policies anyway. Activation duration has no effect on device compliance.

objectives.summary: Conditional Access (CA) is Microsoft Entra's Zero Trust policy engine. It evaluates signals such as user, location, device, application and risk after first-factor authentication, then blocks or grants access with controls like MFA, authentication strength or a compliant device. You need to know how multiple policies combine, how block takes precedence, how report-only mode behaves, and the licensing (P1, with P2 for risk-based policies).

keyFacts.fact: Conditional Access policies are enforced after first-factor authentication completes. They aren't a front-line defense against attacks like denial of service.
When several policies apply to a user, all of them must be satisfied. Within one policy, all assignments are combined with AND.

Enforcement happens in two phases. If any applicable policy uses the Block grant control, enforcement stops and the user is blocked. Otherwise the user is prompted for unmet controls in order, starting with MFA and then a compliant device.
When a policy has multiple grant controls, the default is 'Require all the selected controls'. You can switch to 'Require one of the selected controls'.

Report-only policies are evaluated but never enforce grant or session controls. Users aren't prompted for MFA or blocked, and results such as 'Report-only: User action required' show up in the sign-in logs.

Conditional Access requires Microsoft Entra ID P1. Sign-in risk and user risk policies need Microsoft Entra ID P2 (ID Protection). If the licenses expire, existing policies keep working but can't be updated.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy

lab.title: Require MFA for a pilot group with a report-only rollout
steps: In a trial tenant (Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 trial), sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as a Conditional Access Administrator.
Create a security group named CA-Pilot and add a test user, User1. Create or identify an emergency access account to exclude.
Go to Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy and name it 'Pilot - Require MFA'.
Under Users, include CA-Pilot and exclude the emergency access account.
Under Target resources, include All resources (formerly 'All cloud apps').
Under Grant, select Grant access > Require multifactor authentication, then select Select.
Set Enable policy to Report-only and select Create.
Sign in as User1 in a private window, then review the sign-in log entry's Report-only tab.
After you check the results, change Enable policy to On and sign in again as User1.
lab.verify: In report-only mode, the sign-in log shows the policy as 'Report-only: User action required' and User1 isn't prompted. After you switch the policy to On, User1 is prompted for MFA and the log shows the policy as Success.

questions.scenario: User1 is in scope of three enabled Conditional Access policies for Exchange Online. Policy1 requires MFA. Policy2 requires a compliant device. Policy3 blocks access from locations outside the named location 'HQ'. User1 signs in from a hotel outside HQ on a compliant device and completes MFA.
questions.question: What is the result?
options: Access is granted, because User1 satisfied MFA and device compliance
User1 is prompted to register a new MFA method
Access is granted with a limited session, because the policies conflict
questions.explanation: Every applicable policy must be satisfied, and a policy with the Block control stops enforcement immediately. Policy3 applies because User1 is outside HQ, so access is blocked. Meeting the other two policies doesn't override a block. CA doesn't fall back to a limited session when policies conflict, and nothing in the scenario triggers MFA registration.

objectives.summary: Authentication methods (Microsoft Authenticator, passkeys/FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based authentication, Temporary Access Pass, SMS, voice and more) are managed centrally in the Authentication methods policy. The legacy MFA and SSPR policies can no longer manage methods as of September 30, 2025. Authentication strengths let Conditional Access require specific method combinations, such as phishing-resistant MFA, and Temporary Access Pass bootstraps passwordless registration.

keyFacts.fact: Beginning September 30, 2025, authentication methods can't be managed in the legacy MFA and SSPR policies. Use the Authentication methods policy instead. Authentication Policy Administrator is the least-privileged role that can edit it.

Until migration is complete, a user enabled for a method in any policy (Authentication methods, legacy MFA or legacy SSPR) can register and use it. To block a method you must disable it in all of them. In the 'Migration Complete' state, legacy settings are ignored.

There are three built-in authentication strengths: Multifactor authentication strength, Passwordless MFA strength and Phishing-resistant MFA strength. Phishing-resistant allows Windows Hello for Business or platform credential, FIDO2 security keys and multifactor certificate-based authentication. You can't modify the built-in strengths.

Temporary Access Pass (TAP) policy defaults: minimum lifetime 1 hour, maximum lifetime 8 hours, default lifetime 1 hour, one-time use False, length 8 characters. The allowed lifetime range is 10 minutes to 43,200 minutes (30 days).

You can create a TAP for any user (except external guests, who can't be issued one), but only users included in the TAP authentication method policy can sign in with it. With a one-time TAP, the user must finish registering a passwordless method within 10 minutes of signing in.
Windows Hello for Business satisfies the 'Require multifactor authentication' grant control in Conditional Access.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Entra admin center > Entra ID > Authentication methods > Policies

lab.title: Enable Temporary Access Pass and require phishing-resistant MFA for admins
steps: Sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as an Authentication Policy Administrator.
Go to Entra ID > Authentication methods > Policies and select Temporary Access Pass. Enable it and target a test group, TAP-Users, that contains User1.
Select Configure. Leave the default lifetime at 1 hour and set One-time use to Yes. Select Update, then Save.
In the same Policies list, enable Passkey (FIDO2) for TAP-Users.
As an Authentication Administrator, open User1 > Authentication methods > Add authentication method > Temporary Access Pass and create a pass.
In a private window, sign in as User1 at https://aka.ms/mysecurityinfo with the TAP and register a passkey (if a device or key is available).
As a Conditional Access Administrator, create a report-only CA policy for a test admin group with Grant > Require authentication strength > Phishing-resistant MFA strength.
lab.verify: User1's Authentication methods page lists the TAP (and later the passkey). After one use, the one-time TAP shows as not usable. The CA sign-in log tab shows the authentication strength policy being evaluated.

questions.scenario: Contoso's migration state is Migration in Progress. In the Authentication methods policy, Voice call is enabled only for the group Helpdesk. Users outside Helpdesk are still able to sign in with a voice call.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: Voice call is still enabled in the legacy MFA policy ('Call to phone') or the legacy SSPR policy ('Mobile phone')
Authentication strengths override the Authentication methods policy
Security defaults are turned on and always allow voice calls
Group targeting in the Authentication methods policy is ignored until the policy is 20 KB in size

Users outside the group are most likely enabled through 'Call to phone' in the legacy MFA policy or 'Mobile phone' in the legacy SSPR policy. Authentication strengths restrict methods for a resource, they don't enable extra ones. The scenario doesn't involve security defaults. The 20 KB figure is a policy size limit that can stop you saving the policy, not a targeting threshold.

objectives.summary: An app registration creates the global application object in its home tenant. A service principal (shown under Enterprise applications) is the local instance in each tenant that uses the app, and it controls what the app can do there and who can access it. Securing app identity means choosing strong credentials (federated credentials or certificates rather than client secrets), using 'Assignment required' to limit who gets tokens, and knowing which object to edit for each setting.

keyFacts.fact: An application object has a one-to-many relationship with service principals. One service principal exists in each tenant where the app is used. Registering in the portal creates both automatically, but with Microsoft Graph APIs the service principal is a separate step.
There are three service principal types: application, managed identity and legacy. Managed identity service principals have no app object and can't be modified directly.
Certificates are recommended over client secrets. Client secret lifetime is capped at 24 months, with Microsoft recommending under 12 months. The secret value is shown only once, when you create it.
With 'Assignment required' set to Yes, users and other apps must be assigned to the enterprise app before they can get a token. Global Administrators can sign in regardless of this setting.
Setting 'Enabled for users to sign-in?' to No (accountEnabled=false) stops token issuance for everyone, including service principals that use application permissions.
Deleting an application object also deletes its home-tenant service principal. Restoring the app object through App registrations doesn't restore that service principal.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations (application object); Entra ID > Enterprise apps > All applications > (app) > Properties (service principal)

lab.title: Register an app, add a certificate credential and restrict sign-in
steps: Sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as an Application Administrator.
Go to Entra ID > App registrations > New registration. Name it App1, choose 'Accounts in this organizational directory only' and register it.
Note the Application (client) ID. On the Overview page, select 'Managed application in local directory' to open the service principal.
In App1 > Certificates & secrets, upload a self-signed .cer test certificate. Note the thumbprint.
Optionally, create a client secret with a 6-month expiry and confirm the value is shown only once. Then delete the secret.
Go to Enterprise apps > App1 > Properties, set 'Assignment required?' to Yes and select Save.
Under Users and groups, assign only a test user, User1.
lab.verify: App1 > Certificates & secrets lists the certificate with its thumbprint. The enterprise app Properties page shows 'Assignment required' = Yes. A non-assigned, non-admin user who tries to sign in to the app gets an error saying they aren't assigned.

objectives.summary: Apps get access to data through delegated permissions (on behalf of a signed-in user) or application permissions (app roles, with no user present). User consent settings control whether, and for which apps and permissions, users can consent themselves. The admin consent workflow lets users request approval for anything they can't consent to. You need to know which role can grant which kind of consent, and that application permissions always need admin consent.

keyFacts.fact: By default, every user can consent to permissions that don't require admin consent. The 'microsoft-user-default-low' option limits user consent to apps from verified publishers or registered in your tenant, and to permissions you classify as low impact.
Changing user consent settings only affects future consent. Existing grants stay in place until you revoke them.
Application permissions can only be consented by an admin. They create an appRoleAssignment, while delegated consent creates an oAuth2PermissionGrant.

Privileged Role Administrator can grant tenant-wide admin consent for any permission on any API. Cloud Application Administrator and Application Administrator can grant consent for anything except Microsoft Graph app roles (application permissions).

Being an admin consent workflow reviewer doesn't elevate privileges. Reviewers can view, block or deny requests, but only Global Administrators can approve requests for Microsoft Graph app roles. You need Global Administrator to turn on the workflow.
An app that requires user assignment must have its permissions consented by an administrator, even if user consent policies would otherwise allow it.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > Consent and permissions > User consent settings / Admin consent settings

lab.title: Restrict user consent and enable the admin consent workflow
steps: Sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as a Global Administrator (required for these portal settings in a lab tenant).
Go to Entra ID > Enterprise apps > Consent and permissions > User consent settings.
Select 'Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions' and save.
Open Permission classifications and classify a low-risk delegated permission, such as User.Read, as Low.
Go to Admin consent settings. Set 'Users can request admin consent to apps they are unable to consent to' to Yes.
Add Admin1 as a reviewer, turn on email notifications, set the request expiry to 7 days and save. Allow up to an hour for the change.
As a test user, open an app consent URL that requests a permission requiring admin consent, such as User.Read.All, and submit a request with a justification.
lab.verify: The test user sees 'Approval required' instead of a consent prompt. Admin1 sees the request under Enterprise apps > Admin consent requests > My Pending.

questions.scenario: After a consent-phishing incident at Contoso, Admin1 changes user consent settings from 'Allow user consent for apps' to 'Do not allow user consent'. The next day, the malicious app MailSync can still read the mailboxes of users who consented last week.
questions.question: Why does MailSync still have access, and what should Admin1 do?
options: The change takes 30 days to apply. Wait for it to propagate.
Consent settings only affect future consent. Review and revoke the existing permission grants for MailSync.
User consent settings apply only to multitenant apps. Set Assignment required to Yes instead.
MailSync uses application permissions, which aren't affected by consent. Delete the app registration in Contoso's tenant.
questions.explanation: Changing user consent settings only affects future consent, and existing grants stay in place. Admin1 should review the permissions granted to MailSync and revoke them, and can also disable sign-in for the app. There's no 30-day propagation delay. Consent settings aren't limited to multitenant apps. The scenario describes user consent, which only covers delegated permissions, because users can't consent to application permissions. A third-party app's registration lives in its publisher's tenant, so Contoso can't delete it.

objectives.summary: Managed identities give Azure resources a Microsoft Entra identity that gets tokens without any credentials you have to store or rotate. A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource's lifecycle. A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that can be shared across many resources and survives their deletion. You then grant the identity Azure RBAC roles (or Key Vault data-plane roles) on target resources, and code on the resource gets tokens from the local IMDS endpoint.

keyFacts.fact: A system-assigned identity is deleted along with its resource and can't be shared. A user-assigned identity has its own lifecycle, must be deleted explicitly, and can be attached to multiple resources. Microsoft recommends user-assigned identities for Microsoft services.
To assign a user-assigned identity to a VM, you need Virtual Machine Contributor and Managed Identity Operator role assignments. No Microsoft Entra directory roles are needed.
Creating a user-assigned managed identity needs the Managed Identity Contributor role. Listing or reading one needs Managed Identity Operator or Managed Identity Contributor.

On a VM, code requests tokens from IMDS at http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token with the header Metadata: true. If several user-assigned identities are attached, pass client_id, object_id or msi_res_id.
Managed identity tokens are cached by the back end for about 24 hours per resource URI, so permission changes can take hours to take effect. You can't force a refresh.
A user-assigned managed identity can't be moved to a different resource group. You have to create a new one and grant its permissions again.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > (VM) > Security > Identity > System assigned / User assigned

lab.title: Give a VM's managed identity read access to a resource group
steps: In a free or trial subscription, create resource group RG1 and a small Linux VM, VM1, with a public IP or Bastion.
Open VM1 > Security > Identity > System assigned, set Status to On and save. Note the Object (principal) ID.
Open RG1 > Access control (IAM) > Add role assignment. Choose Reader, select Managed identity > Virtual machine > VM1 and save.
SSH to VM1 and run: curl 'http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=2018-02-01&resource=https://management.azure.com/' -H Metadata:true
Copy access_token and call: curl https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/RG1?api-version=2016-09-01 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

objectives.summary: Deploying Key Vault involves choosing a globally unique name, a tier (Standard or Premium) and an access model, and setting protections such as purge protection at creation time. Choose Standard for software-protected keys, Premium for HSM-protected keys, and Managed HSM when you need a single-tenant HSM with a customer-controlled root of trust. Microsoft recommends one vault per application per environment.

keyFacts.fact: A key vault name must be 3 to 24 characters and can contain only numbers, letters and hyphens. The vault URI is https://<vault-name>.vault.azure.net/.
Standard tier uses software libraries validated to FIPS 140 Level 1. Premium tier adds HSM-protected keys generated and protected by FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs.

Managed HSM is single-tenant and FIPS 140-3 Level 3, with a customer-controlled security domain as the root of trust. Standard and Premium vaults are multitenant, with Microsoft controlling the root of trust. Managed HSM supports only HSM-backed keys.
Premium vaults can hold both software-protected and HSM-protected keys, so you have to check that a key you create is actually HSM-protected.
Microsoft recommends one vault per application per environment (Development, Pre-Production, Production), with roles assigned at the vault scope.

With Key Vault API version 2026-02-01 or later, newly created vaults default to Azure RBAC (enableRbacAuthorization = true). Existing vaults keep their current model. Older control plane API versions retire on February 27, 2027.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Key vaults > Create > Basics (name, region, pricing tier, soft-delete retention, purge protection) > Access configuration > Networking

Run: az group create --name rg-kv-lab --location eastus
Run: az keyvault create --name <unique-name> --resource-group rg-kv-lab --enable-rbac-authorization true --enable-purge-protection true
Note the Vault URI in the output (https://<unique-name>.vault.azure.net/).
Run: az keyvault show --name <unique-name> --query "{rbac:properties.enableRbacAuthorization, purge:properties.enablePurgeProtection, sku:properties.sku.name}"

Managed HSM would also meet FIPS 140-3 Level 3, but it's single-tenant with a customer-owned security domain, which the scenario doesn't require.

objectives.summary: Key Vault settings include soft-delete retention, purge protection, and the 'Enable access to' options that let Azure services such as Virtual Machines, Resource Manager and Disk Encryption retrieve secrets. Soft-delete is always on for new vaults. Purge protection is optional but is required by many CMK integrations. Retention and purge protection can't be undone, which makes them common exam traps.

keyFacts.fact: Soft-delete is on by default for new vaults and can't be disabled once enabled. Deleted vaults and objects can be recovered for 7 to 90 days, with 90 days as the default.
The retention period can only be set when the vault is created and can't be changed later. The same interval applies to soft-delete and purge protection.

Purge protection is off by default and requires soft-delete. Once it's on, deleted vaults and objects can't be purged until the retention period passes, but they can still be recovered. Services such as Azure Storage need it for customer-managed keys.
To purge a soft-deleted object you need purge permission, for example the Key Vault Purge Operator role. You can't reuse a soft-deleted vault's name until the retention period expires.
Soft-deleting a vault deletes integrated items such as Azure RBAC role assignments and Event Grid subscriptions. Recovering the vault doesn't restore them.

enabledForDiskEncryption is required for Azure Disk Encryption. enabledForDeployment lets Microsoft.Compute retrieve secrets, such as certificates, when creating VMs. enabledForTemplateDeployment lets Resource Manager get secrets referenced in template deployments.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Key vault > Settings > Properties (soft-delete, purge protection) and Access configuration (Azure Virtual Machines for deployment, Azure Resource Manager for template deployment, Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption)

lab.title: Test soft-delete, recovery and Disk Encryption access
steps: Create a vault with a 7-day retention period and without purge protection: az keyvault create -n <name> -g rg-kv-lab --retention-days 7
Assign yourself Key Vault Secrets Officer on the vault, then run: az keyvault secret set --vault-name <name> -n Secret1 --value Test123
Delete the secret: az keyvault secret delete --vault-name <name> -n Secret1
List deleted secrets: az keyvault secret list-deleted --vault-name <name>
Recover it: az keyvault secret recover --vault-name <name> -n Secret1
Enable Disk Encryption access: az keyvault update -n <name> -g rg-kv-lab --enabled-for-disk-encryption true
Turn on purge protection: az keyvault update -n <name> -g rg-kv-lab --enable-purge-protection true. Then try to turn it off in the portal.
lab.verify: Secret1 shows in list-deleted after the delete and returns after recover. az keyvault show reports enabledForDiskEncryption = true and enablePurgeProtection = true. The portal doesn't let you disable purge protection.

objectives.summary: Key Vault has a control plane (managing the vault through management.azure.com, always authorized with Azure RBAC) and a data plane (keys, secrets and certificates through <vault>.vault.azure.net, authorized with Azure RBAC or legacy access policies). Exam questions focus on choosing the least-privileged data-plane role, on the fact that control-plane roles like Key Vault Contributor don't grant data access, and on the access-policy escalation risk.

keyFacts.fact: Key Vault Secrets User can read secret contents, including the secret portion of a certificate with a private key. Key Vault Secrets Officer can do anything with secrets except manage permissions.
Key Vault Reader can read metadata of vaults and their objects but can't read sensitive values such as secret contents or key material.
Key Vault Contributor is control plane only. It lets you manage vaults but doesn't give access to keys, secrets or certificates.
With the access policy model, anyone with Contributor rights on the vault's control plane can grant themselves data-plane access by setting an access policy. Limit who holds Contributor.

Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User can read key metadata and do wrap and unwrap. It's the role for service-side CMK encryption. Key Vault Crypto User can perform cryptographic operations with keys.

Switching a vault to the Azure RBAC permission model invalidates all access policy permissions. It needs unrestricted Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write (Owner, or User Access Administrator plus vaults/write). Key Vault Data Access Administrator can't change the permission model.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Key vault > Access control (IAM) > Add role assignment (RBAC model); Key vault > Settings > Access configuration (choose permission model)

lab.title: Grant least-privileged secret access to a managed identity
steps: Use an RBAC-enabled vault, KV1, and a VM or App Service that has a system-assigned managed identity.
Assign yourself Key Vault Secrets Officer on KV1 and create a secret: az keyvault secret set --vault-name KV1 -n DbPassword --value P@ss1
Assign the managed identity read-only secret access: az role assignment create --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --assignee <principal-id> --scope $(az keyvault show -n KV1 --query id -o tsv)
Assign a test user Key Vault Reader on KV1.
Sign in as the test user and try az keyvault secret show --vault-name KV1 -n DbPassword.
On the VM, sign in with az login --identity and run az keyvault secret show --vault-name KV1 -n DbPassword.

questions.question: How was this possible, and what's the recommended fix?

Contributor can change vault access policies on the control plane and grant itself data-plane access. Migrate KV2 to Azure RBAC and limit who holds Contributor.
Access policies are inherited from the resource group. Delete the resource group policy.
The vault firewall was disabled. Enable 'Disable public access' to fix the problem.
questions.explanation: Under the access policy model, setting access policies is a control-plane operation, so a user with Contributor can add an access policy for themselves and then read secrets. The fix is to tightly limit who holds Contributor and move to Azure RBAC, where Contributor and Key Vault Contributor don't grant data access. Contributor doesn't directly include secret read, which is why option A is wrong, and removing Reader wouldn't help anyway. Access policies aren't inherited from resource groups. Network settings don't fix an authorization problem.

options: Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User
questions.explanation: Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User is limited to reading key metadata and doing wrap and unwrap, which is exactly what service-side CMK encryption needs. Crypto Officer can manage keys, Key Vault Administrator covers all data-plane operations, and both go beyond least privilege. Secrets User applies to secrets, not keys.

objectives.summary: The Key Vault firewall restricts data-plane access to selected public IPv4 ranges, virtual network subnets (service endpoints), private endpoints and, optionally, trusted Microsoft services. Exam questions test the defaults, the limits, the fact that private RFC 1918 addresses can't be used in IP rules, how trusted-service bypass behaves when public access is disabled or Network Security Perimeter is used, and that firewall rules don't apply to control-plane operations.

keyFacts.fact: By default, the Key Vault firewall is disabled for new vaults. Requests are still authenticated with Microsoft Entra ID and authorized with RBAC or access policies.
You can have up to 200 virtual network rules and 1,000 IPv4 rules. IP rules accept public IPv4 addresses only. Private RFC 1918 ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) and IPv6 aren't allowed.
To allow a subnet, enable the Microsoft.KeyVault service endpoint on it, add a network rule, and set the default action to Deny. Service endpoint changes can take up to 15 minutes to apply.

'Allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass this firewall' still applies when publicNetworkAccess is Disabled. If the vault is set to 'Secure by perimeter' (Network Security Perimeter), even trusted services are blocked unless a perimeter access rule allows them.
Some services, such as Azure DevOps, aren't on the trusted services list. They're blocked whether or not the bypass is enabled, and should connect through a private endpoint or an allowed network.
Firewall rules apply only to data-plane operations. Control-plane operations, including deploying secrets through ARM templates via management.azure.com, aren't restricted by them.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Key vault > Networking > Firewalls and virtual networks (Allow access from: All networks / Selected networks / Disable public access; Exception: Allow trusted Microsoft services)

lab.title: Lock a vault to one subnet and your public IP
steps: Create VNet1 with subnet App: az network vnet create -g rg-kv-lab -n VNet1 --subnet-name App
Enable the service endpoint: az network vnet subnet update -g rg-kv-lab --vnet-name VNet1 -n App --service-endpoints Microsoft.KeyVault
Add the subnet rule: az keyvault network-rule add -g rg-kv-lab -n <vault> --subnet $(az network vnet subnet show -g rg-kv-lab --vnet-name VNet1 -n App --query id -o tsv)
Add your public IP: az keyvault network-rule add -g rg-kv-lab -n <vault> --ip-address <your-public-ip>/32
Allow trusted services: az keyvault update -g rg-kv-lab -n <vault> --bypass AzureServices
Set the default action to Deny: az keyvault update -g rg-kv-lab -n <vault> --default-action Deny
From a network that isn't allowed (for example a phone hotspot), open the vault's Secrets blade in the portal.

objectives.summary: Key Vault stores keys (RSA and EC, plus HSM-protected keys and symmetric oct-HSM keys in preview on Premium), secrets (any value up to the size limits) and certificates (X.509 with a policy-driven lifecycle). Exam-relevant management tasks include key rotation policies, certificate auto-renewal through integrated CAs, how certificates map to an addressable key and secret, and what object attributes like expiry actually enforce.

keyFacts.fact: A key rotation policy creates a new key version automatically. The minimum rotation time is 7 days after creation and 7 days before expiry. Managing the rotation policy requires Key Vault Crypto Officer, or the Rotate, Set Rotation Policy and Get Rotation Policy permissions in the access policy model.
Services should reference a versionless key URI so they pick up rotated versions automatically. Keep old key versions enabled until data encryption keys have been rewrapped.

Creating a Key Vault certificate also creates an addressable key and secret with the same name. The secret returns the certificate value, including the private key if it's exportable. HSM keys are never exportable.

Key Vault auto-renews certificates end to end only for its partnered (integrated) CAs, DigiCert and GlobalSign, and for self-signed certificates. New certificates default to a 12-month validity and auto-renew at 80% of their lifetime. Certificates from non-partnered CAs need manual renewal (new version, CSR, merge).
A secret's exp and nbf attributes are informational. A get operation still works on expired and not-yet-valid secrets. Set enabled = false to block retrieval.
Certificate contacts are shared by every certificate in the vault and are notified of lifecycle events such as expiry and renewal.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Key vault > Objects > Keys (Rotation policy) / Secrets / Certificates (Issuance Policy, Certificate Contacts)

lab.title: Configure a key rotation policy and a self-signed certificate
steps: Assign yourself Key Vault Crypto Officer and Key Vault Certificates Officer on an RBAC-enabled vault.
Create a key: az keyvault key create --vault-name <vault> -n Key1 --kty RSA --size 3072
Save policy.json with a lifetimeActions entry {trigger: {timeAfterCreate: 'P18M'}, action: {type: 'Rotate'}}, a Notify action at timeBeforeExpiry 'P30D', and attributes expiryTime 'P2Y'.
Apply it: az keyvault key rotation-policy update --vault-name <vault> -n Key1 --value policy.json
Rotate on demand: az keyvault key rotate --vault-name <vault> -n Key1
Create a self-signed certificate: az keyvault certificate create --vault-name <vault> -n Cert1 -p "$(az keyvault certificate get-default-policy)"
Run az keyvault secret show --vault-name <vault> -n Cert1 --query contentType
lab.verify: az keyvault key list-versions shows two versions of Key1. Cert1 also appears as a key and a secret with the same name, and the secret's content type is PKCS #12 (the default).

questions.scenario: Contoso stores TLS certificates in KV1. The certificates come from an internal enterprise CA that isn't partnered with Key Vault. Admin1 sets the lifetime action to 'Automatically renew at a given time'.
questions.question: What should Admin1 expect?
options: Key Vault renews the certificates automatically with the internal CA
Autorotation doesn't apply to certificates from non-partnered CAs. Renewal must be done manually or with custom automation.
The certificates are automatically reissued by DigiCert
Key Vault converts the certificates to self-signed certificates at renewal
questions.explanation: Key Vault autorotates certificates through its CA partnerships with DigiCert and GlobalSign, so autorotation doesn't apply to non-partnered CAs, which need manual renewal or custom automation. Key Vault can't request renewals from an arbitrary internal CA, won't move certificates to DigiCert on its own, and doesn't convert certificates to self-signed.

questions.question: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.

statements.text: KV2 now also contains a key and a secret named WebCert.
A get operation on ApiKey fails because the secret has expired.
If WebCert had been created with an RSA-HSM key, its private key could be exported through the WebCert secret.

questions.explanation: Statement 1 is Yes. Creating a certificate also creates an addressable key and secret with the same name. Statement 2 is No. A secret's exp attribute is informational, and get still works on expired secrets. Statement 3 is No. HSM keys are non-exportable, so the private key isn't included in the secret value.

questions.scenario: KV3 holds a CMK used by several Azure services. Security requires a new key version every 12 months, no service outages, and an Event Grid notice 30 days before expiry. Key1 already has an expiration date set.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Create a rotation policy with a Rotate action at timeAfterCreate P12M. Add a Notify action at timeBeforeExpiry P30D, set expiryTime in the policy, and make sure the services use the versionless key URI.
Create a rotation policy with only a Notify action, and rotate manually each year by deleting and recreating Key1
Disable the old key version immediately after each rotation to force services to update
Set Key1's exp attribute to 12 months. Key Vault rotates keys automatically when they expire.
questions.explanation: A Rotate action triggered 12 months after creation produces new versions on schedule. The Notify action needs an expiry time in the rotation policy and an expiration date on the key: Key1 already has one, and the policy's expiryTime sets the expiration date on each newly rotated version. Services that use the versionless key URI pick up new versions without outages. Deleting and recreating the key breaks services that depend on it. Disabling old versions too early causes outages, because data encryption keys must be rewrapped first. Expiry doesn't trigger rotation; only a rotation policy (or on-demand rotation) does.

objectives.summary: Defender for Cloud's secrets scanning finds exposed plaintext credentials, such as SSH private keys, storage connection strings, SAS tokens, Entra client secrets and cloud access keys, so you can move them into Key Vault before attackers use them for lateral movement. There are three scanning types: agentless machine scanning (Defender CSPM or Defender for Servers Plan 2), cloud deployment resource scanning (Defender CSPM), and code repository scanning in Azure DevOps or GitHub (relies on GitHub Advanced Security). Findings appear in recommendations, inventory, cloud security explorer and attack paths.

keyFacts.fact: Agentless machine secrets scanning is available with either Defender CSPM or Defender for Servers Plan 2. Cloud deployment resource scanning and code repository scanning are listed under Defender CSPM.
Machine secrets scanning takes disk snapshots and analyzes them out-of-band, with no agent and no effect on VM performance. It covers Azure VMs and connected AWS and GCP instances.

To turn it on, go to Environment settings > subscription > Settings for Defender CSPM or Defender for Servers Plan 2, and enable 'Agentless scanning for machines'. Scans run every 24 hours and only cover machines that are running.

To scan VMs with CMK-encrypted disks, grant the Microsoft Defender for Cloud Servers Scanner Resource Provider Get, Wrap Key and Unwrap Key access in the access policy model, or the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role in the RBAC model.

Cloud deployment secrets scanning is agentless and reads deployment metadata (templates, parameters, outputs) through the cloud control plane API. It catches secrets that only appear at deployment time.

Code repository secret scanning relies on GitHub Advanced Security. Viewing the findings is part of Foundational CSPM, but tracing lateral movement to runtime resources needs Defender CSPM, and attack paths for exposed secrets currently cover Azure DevOps repositories only.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > (subscription) > Defender plans > Defender CSPM > Settings > Agentless scanning for machines

lab.title: Detect a plaintext secret on a VM with Defender CSPM
steps: In a trial subscription, open Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings and select the subscription.
Turn on the Defender CSPM plan, select Settings, and make sure 'Agentless scanning for machines' is On. Save.
Create a small Linux VM, VM1, and keep it running.

On VM1, create a test file containing a fake storage connection string, for example DefaultEndpointsProtocol=https;AccountName=fakeacct;AccountKey=<random base64>;EndpointSuffix=core.windows.net. Don't use a real key.
Wait up to 24 hours for the next scheduled scan.
Open Recommendations and search for 'Machines should have secrets findings resolved'. Also open Cloud security explorer and run a VM secrets template query.
lab.verify: VM1 is listed under the 'Machines should have secrets findings resolved' recommendation or in cloud security explorer results, with the discovered secret type. Delete the test file and VM afterward.

objectives.summary: Microsoft Defender for Key Vault is the Defender for Cloud plan that detects unusual and potentially harmful attempts to access or exploit key vaults, such as access from TOR exit nodes or suspicious IPs, unusual users or apps, and secret-dumping patterns. You enable it per subscription under Environment settings. Alerts appear on the vault's Security page and in Defender for Cloud. The response flow is to identify the source, contain it with the firewall or permission changes, measure impact, and rotate any affected secrets.

keyFacts.fact: Defender for Key Vault is generally available. You enable it under Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > (subscription) > Defender plans by setting Key Vault to On. Defender for Cloud must be enabled on the subscription first.
Alerts appear on the key vault's Security page, in Workload protections and on Defender for Cloud's Security alerts page, and can also be emailed.

Example alerts include Access from a TOR exit node (KV_TORAccess), Suspicious policy change and secret query (KV_PutGetAnomaly), Suspicious secret listing and query (KV_ListGetAnomaly, associated with secret dumping) and Unusual application accessed a key vault (KV_AppAnomaly).
Alerts include the Object ID and the UPN or IP. If an app accessed the vault there's no UPN, and if traffic came from outside Azure there's no Object ID.

Don't dismiss an alert just because you recognize the user or app, since the plan is designed to catch stolen credentials. Verify with the owner, and use a suppression rule if you need to reduce noise.
Recommended response: enable the Key Vault firewall for unrecognized IPs, remove or restrict suspicious principals, review which secrets were accessed, then rotate, disable or delete them.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > (subscription) > Defender plans > Key Vault = On

objectives.summary: Azure Policy evaluates resources against built-in or custom definitions and applies an effect such as audit, deny, modify or deployIfNotExists. The exam tests the effect evaluation order, which effects change existing resources, and the managed identity and remediation task that modify and deployIfNotExists need. Custom definitions also need the right mode (all or indexed).

keyFacts.fact: Effect evaluation order on create/update requests: disabled first, then append and modify, then deny, then audit, then manual, auditIfNotExists, and denyAction last. auditIfNotExists and deployIfNotExists run again after the resource provider returns success.

In Resource Manager mode, deny stops a non-compliant create or update request before it reaches the resource provider and returns 403 (Forbidden). Existing resources that match are only flagged as non-compliant. Nothing is deleted.

Assignments that use modify or deployIfNotExists act through a managed identity, either system-assigned or user-assigned, and each assignment can have only one. The portal grants the roles listed in roleDefinitionIds automatically. With an SDK, PowerShell or CLI you must grant those roles yourself.

Existing non-compliant resources are not changed automatically. A remediation task applies the modify operations or deploys the deployIfNotExists template to them. A task can be created from Policy > Remediation, from a non-compliant assignment, or while assigning at subscription scope.

Custom definition mode: 'all' evaluates resource groups, subscriptions and all resource types. 'indexed' evaluates only types that support tags and location, so use it for tag or location policies. Definitions created in the portal use 'all'.

Timing: a new assignment takes about 5 minutes to apply to its scope. A single created or updated resource shows its compliance about 15 minutes later. Every assignment is reevaluated automatically once every 24 hours.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Policy > Authoring > Definitions (create custom definitions) or Assignments > Assign policy; Policy > Remediation > Policies to remediate

lab.title: Audit, then deny, storage accounts that allow Shared Key access

Under Authoring, select Assignments > Assign policy.

For Policy definition, search for 'shared key access' and select 'Storage accounts should prevent shared key access'. Keep the effect at Audit, then select Review + create > Create.
Create a storage account in the resource group with 'Allow storage account key access' left enabled.
After the evaluation runs, open the assignment and select View compliance. The storage account should be listed as non-compliant.
Edit the assignment. On the Parameters tab, clear 'Only show parameters that need input or review', change Effect from Audit to Deny, and save.
Wait up to 30 minutes, then try to create another storage account with Shared Key access allowed.

flashcards.front: Why is deny evaluated before audit?
flashcards.back: So that an unwanted resource isn't logged twice. append and modify run even earlier, because they can change the request so that it no longer triggers deny or audit.

items: disabled
modify (with append)
deny
audit
questions.explanation: disabled comes first and decides whether the rule is evaluated at all. append and modify come next because they can change the request, which might stop deny or audit from triggering. deny runs before audit so that an unwanted resource isn't logged twice. audit follows. auditIfNotExists and deployIfNotExists run only after the resource provider returns success, so they come after all four.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam assigned a built-in policy with the modify effect to Subscription1. The policy adds a CostCenter tag. New resources get the tag, but 120 resources that existed before the assignment are still listed as non-compliant.
questions.question: What should you do to bring the existing resources into compliance?
options: Change the assignment effect to deny.
Create a remediation task for the policy assignment.
Wait for the standard 24-hour compliance evaluation cycle.
Create a policy exemption for the resource group that contains the resources.
questions.explanation: A modify policy changes new and updated requests, but existing resources stay non-compliant until a remediation task runs the modify operations through the assignment's managed identity. Deny only blocks future non-compliant requests and never changes existing resources. The 24-hour cycle only reevaluates and reports compliance. An exemption removes the resources from evaluation, which hides the problem rather than adding the tag.

objectives.summary: The Defender for Cloud Regulatory compliance dashboard scores your environment against standards such as the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB), ISO 27001 or PCI DSS. Each standard is backed by an Azure Policy initiative. You need to know which standard is there by default, what you need before you can add others, why some controls are grayed out, and how quickly results refresh.

keyFacts.fact: By default the regulatory compliance dashboard shows only the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. Any other standard has to be added to the dashboard explicitly.

Adding a compliance standard requires an onboarded Defender for Cloud plan. Defender for Servers Plan 1 and Defender for API Plan 1 don't qualify. You also need Owner or Policy Contributor permissions.

Regulatory compliance standards in Defender for Cloud are built on Azure Policy initiatives. Microsoft recommends assigning them at the highest applicable scope so compliance data rolls up for all nested resources.
Compliance assessments run about every 12 hours, so a fix appears in the dashboard only after the next assessment run.

A grayed-out control has no automated Defender for Cloud assessment. It might be procedural or a platform responsibility. A standard that is assigned but has no relevant resources doesn't appear on the dashboard at all.
The Reader role on a subscription can read policy compliance data, but the Security Reader role can't.

Find a standard such as ISO 27001 and set its status to On. Fill in any parameters the Set parameters page asks for.
Back on Regulatory compliance, select the standard, expand a control, and select Control details.
Review the Overview, Your Actions and Microsoft Actions tabs, and open a failing automated assessment to see its remediation steps.
lab.verify: After the next assessment run (about 12 hours), the standard appears on the Regulatory compliance dashboard for your subscription. It appears only if the subscription has relevant resources.

objectives.summary: In Defender for Cloud, security policies are made of standards: security benchmarks such as MCSB, regulatory standards, and custom standards. Resources that fail a standard's controls produce recommendations. For this objective, know how to manage recommendation effects (Audit, Deny, Disabled, Enforce), when to use exemptions, and which plan custom recommendations require.

keyFacts.fact: A Defender for Cloud security policy can contain security benchmarks (for example MCSB), regulatory compliance standards, and custom standards. A resource that fails a control generates a security recommendation.
Custom recommendations are written in KQL inside a custom standard. They need the Defender CSPM plan and work for all clouds.

Deny blocks deployment of resources that don't comply with MCSB. Enforce uses the Azure Policy DeployIfNotExists effect to remediate resources automatically when they're created. Both work only for Azure and only on a subset of recommendations.
Security Reader can view recommendations, alerts and policy. Security Admin can also update security policies and dismiss alerts.

An exemption is categorized as 'Resolved through third-party service (mitigated)' or 'Risk accepted (waiver)' and can have an expiration date. Exempted resources show as Not applicable. The limit is 5,000 resource exemptions per subscription, and exemptions should be created in Defender for Cloud rather than through the Azure Policy API.

Within a security control, a resource adds points only when all of the control's recommendations are remediated for that resource. Fixing some of the recommendations for a resource doesn't change the score, and the control's maximum points need every recommendation fixed on every resource.

objectives.summary: Management locks (CanNotDelete and ReadOnly) protect subscriptions, resource groups and resources from accidental deletion or change, and they override the permissions of every user. Locks are inherited, and the most restrictive one wins. Questions usually turn on two facts: locks apply only to control-plane operations, and a ReadOnly lock can break operations you might not expect, because it blocks POST calls such as listing storage account keys.

keyFacts.fact: CanNotDelete (called Delete in the portal) lets authorized users read and modify a resource but not delete it. ReadOnly (Read-only in the portal) lets them only read it, which is similar to restricting everyone to the Reader role. Both override user permissions.

A lock on a parent scope is inherited by every child resource, including resources added later, and the most restrictive lock wins. A Delete lock on one resource makes deletion of its resource group fail completely, because partial deletes don't happen.
Locks apply only to control-plane operations sent to management.azure.com. A lock on a storage account doesn't stop data-plane operations such as deleting blobs.

A ReadOnly lock on a storage account blocks List Keys, which is a POST request, and blocks new Azure RBAC role assignments scoped to the account or its containers. Users then need Microsoft Entra credentials to reach blob or queue data.
Creating or deleting locks requires Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions. Owner and User Access Administrator have them, and Contributor doesn't.
Management groups can't be locked. A resource lock doesn't prevent a subscription from being canceled.

objectives.portalPath: Resource, resource group or subscription > Settings > Locks (called Resource locks on a subscription) > Add

lab.title: Prove that a resource group lock blocks deletion
steps: In Cloud Shell (Bash), run: az group create --name rg-locklab --location eastus
Create any small resource in the group, for example a storage account.
Run: az lock create --name LockGroup --lock-type CanNotDelete --resource-group rg-locklab
Run: az lock list --resource-group rg-locklab and confirm the lock is listed.
Try to delete the group: az group delete --name rg-locklab --yes
Remove the lock: lockid=$(az lock show --name LockGroup --resource-group rg-locklab --output tsv --query id) and then az lock delete --ids $lockid
Delete the group again to clean up.
lab.verify: The first az group delete fails with an error saying the scope is locked. After you delete the lock, the group deletes successfully.

objectives.summary: A built-in Azure role assignment combines a security principal, a role definition and a scope. The exam expects you to tell the privileged administrator roles apart (Owner, Contributor, User Access Administrator, Role Based Access Control Administrator) and to delegate role assignment safely by adding conditions. You should also know the per-subscription limit on role assignments.

keyFacts.fact: Owner has full resource access and can assign roles. Contributor has full resource access but can't assign roles. User Access Administrator and Role Based Access Control Administrator both manage access and can even assign Owner. RBAC Administrator can't manage access by other means, such as Azure Policy.

A role assignment has three parts: security principal, role definition and scope. Scope can be a management group, subscription, resource group or resource, and child scopes inherit assignments from their parents.
Microsoft recommends no more than 3 subscription owners and recommends assigning roles to groups instead of individual users.

A subscription can hold at most 5,000 role assignments, counting those at subscription, resource group and resource scope but not management group scope. Eligible and future-scheduled assignments don't count, and the limit can't be raised.

To delegate role assignment without handing out broad power, assign Role Based Access Control Administrator, User Access Administrator or Owner with a condition that limits which roles the user can assign and to which principals.
Removing a role assignment requires Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete, which Role Based Access Control Administrator has, for example.

objectives.summary: Custom roles fill the gaps built-in roles leave. Azure custom roles, in Azure RBAC, control access to Azure resources. Microsoft Entra custom roles control directory objects such as app registrations. Expect questions on AssignableScopes rules and limits, the DataActions restriction at management group scope, NotActions not being a deny, and licensing and admin requirements on the Entra side.

keyFacts.fact: A tenant can have up to 5,000 Azure custom roles. AssignableScopes can't be the root scope ("/") or contain wildcards, and it can name only one management group.
A custom role that includes DataActions can't be assigned at management group scope. You can still list one management group in AssignableScopes and assign the role at the subscriptions under it.
NotActions isn't a deny. Effective permissions are Actions minus NotActions, and if a second role grants the excluded action, the user can perform it. Only deny assignments block access.
To create, update or delete an Azure custom role you need Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions/write on all of its AssignableScopes, which Owner and User Access Administrator have, for example.
Microsoft Entra custom roles need a Microsoft Entra ID P1 license for every user with a custom role assignment. Built-in Entra roles are free.

Privileged Role Administrator is enough to create Microsoft Entra custom roles. In the admin center you can clone permissions from another custom role but not from a built-in role. A custom role with app registration permissions can be assigned at directory (tenant) scope or scoped to a single app registration.

objectives.summary: Overprivileged access means permanent, broad or unused role assignments that widen the blast radius when an identity is compromised. You find them with Defender for Cloud identity recommendations and the CIEM capabilities in Defender CSPM, and with the Privileged tab on Access control (IAM). You fix them by removing assignments, swapping privileged roles for job-function roles, narrowing scope, adding conditions, and using PIM for just-in-time access.

keyFacts.fact: The CIEM capabilities in Defender for Cloud come with the Defender CSPM plan. They analyze identity configuration and usage across Azure, AWS and GCP and recommend right-sizing overprovisioned identities and removing inactive, guest or blocked accounts.

Built-in identity recommendations include: at most 3 owners per subscription; remove blocked accounts that have owner permissions; don't give service principals administrative roles at subscription or resource group level; revoke access from identities with no activity in the past 45 days.

Best practice for privileged administrator roles: remove assignments that aren't needed, use a job function role where one fits, assign at a narrow scope such as a resource group or resource, and add conditions to roles that can create role assignments.
A role counts as privileged if it includes *, */write, */delete, or write or delete actions on roleAssignments, roleDefinitions or denyAssignments.

Access control (IAM) > Role assignments > Privileged lists the privileged administrator assignments at a scope. From View assignments you can add a condition or remove an assignment. Download role assignments exports the list to CSV or JSON.
Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management provides just-in-time, time-bound access to Azure resources, after which the privileges are revoked automatically.

Select Download role assignments, include 'At current scope', choose CSV, and select Start. Review the file.

objectives.summary: Azure Backup has layered defenses against ransomware and rogue administrators. Soft delete keeps deleted backups recoverable. Immutable vaults block operations that would lose recovery points. Multi-user authorization (MUA) through a Resource Guard requires a second party to approve critical operations. Know the retention ranges, which settings are reversible, and which operations are mandatory versus optional under MUA.

keyFacts.fact: Soft-delete retention can be set from 14 to 180 days and defaults to 14 days, which incur no retention cost. Soft delete is now enforced by default (secure by default): it's generally available for Recovery Services vaults, where it can't be disabled, and for Backup vaults it's GA in some regions and in preview in the rest.

An immutable vault is Disabled, Enabled (blocks operations that lose backups, but can be turned off again) or Enabled and locked (irreversible, with WORM storage). Recovery Services vaults and Backup vaults both support it.

In an immutable Recovery Services vault, stopping protection with data deletion and reducing backup policy retention are blocked, while increasing retention is still allowed (with the 'specific duration' option, retention can be reduced only down to the immutability duration). Immutability doesn't apply to operational backups of blobs, files and disks.
Under MUA, 'Disable soft delete' and 'Remove MUA protection' are mandatory protected operations and can't be excluded. Restore is optional and isn't protected by default.

To enable MUA on a vault, the Backup admin needs the Reader role on the Resource Guard or on its subscription, and the Resource Guard must be in the same region as the vault. For stronger isolation, create the Resource Guard in a separate subscription or tenant.
Disabling MUA on a Backup vault is itself protected. The Backup admin needs the Backup MUA Operator role on the Resource Guard, ideally granted just-in-time through PIM.

lab.title: Harden a Recovery Services vault
steps: Create a Recovery Services vault in a test resource group.
Go to Properties > Security Settings > Update. Confirm soft delete is enabled and set the retention to 30 days. Don't choose always-on in a lab, because it can't be undone.
Under Properties > Immutable vault, enable immutability but don't lock it, so you can reverse it later.
Search for Resource Guards and create one in the same region as the vault. On Protected operations, review which operations can be disabled.
On the Resource Guard, open Access control (IAM) and assign the Reader role to the account acting as Backup admin.
In the vault, go to Properties > Multi-User Authorization > Update, select the Resource Guard, select Authenticate, and save.
Try to disable soft delete on the vault.
lab.verify: The vault properties show immutability as Enabled and MUA as protected by your Resource Guard. The attempt to disable soft delete fails with an authorization error unless you hold permissions on the Resource Guard.

objectives.summary: Infrastructure as code (Bicep, ARM, Terraform) lets you build security controls into every deployment and catch misconfigurations before they reach production. Know the Microsoft Security DevOps (MSDO) scanners and which template languages each covers, how Defender for Cloud shows IaC findings, how to preview changes with what-if, and how to declare controls such as locks and Defender for Storage settings in templates.

keyFacts.fact: The IaC scanners in Microsoft Security DevOps are Template Analyzer (ARM and Bicep, with PSRule included), Checkov and Terrascan. To scan only IaC, add categories: 'IaC' to the GitHub action or the Azure DevOps task.
MSDO IaC scan results appear in Defender for Cloud > DevOps security, which doesn't need a GitHub Advanced Security license. With GHAS they also show under Security > Code scanning alerts in GitHub.
Agentless code scanning (preview) uses the GitHub or Azure DevOps connector with no pipeline changes. It scans code and IaC on the default branch after connector creation and then daily.

The what-if operation predicts what a Bicep deployment will change without changing anything. Run it with az deployment group what-if, or use --confirm-with-what-if to review and confirm before deploying.
Locks can be declared in Bicep or ARM as Microsoft.Authorization/locks. Leave out the scope property to lock the deployment scope, such as the resource group, and set scope to lock a single resource.
Defender for Storage can be enabled with Bicep, ARM or Terraform at subscription or storage account level. Setting the malware scanning cap parameter to -1 allows unlimited scanning.

lab.title: Deploy a hardened storage account with Bicep and what-if
steps: In Cloud Shell, create a resource group: az group create --name rg-iaclab --location eastus
Create main.bicep with a Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource whose properties set allowBlobPublicAccess: false, allowSharedKeyAccess: false and minimumTlsVersion: 'TLS1_2'.
In the same file, add a Microsoft.Authorization/locks resource with level 'CanNotDelete' and scope set to the storage account.
Preview the deployment: az deployment group what-if --resource-group rg-iaclab --template-file main.bicep
Deploy with confirmation: az deployment group create --resource-group rg-iaclab --confirm-with-what-if --template-file main.bicep
Run: az storage account show --name <account> --resource-group rg-iaclab --query allowSharedKeyAccess
lab.verify: What-if lists the storage account and lock as resources to create. After deployment the query returns false, and az lock list --resource-group rg-iaclab shows the CanNotDelete lock.

objectives.summary: Storage account hardening comes down to a handful of account-level settings: secure transfer (HTTPS), minimum TLS version, blob anonymous access, Shared Key authorization, and the encryption options. The exam often tests the defaults, especially those that differ between the portal and CLI/ARM. It also tests what each setting overrides and which roles can change it, so it's worth knowing that Storage Account Contributor can list the account keys.

keyFacts.fact: If AllowSharedKeyAccess isn't set (null) or is true, the account accepts Shared Key requests. Setting it to false rejects requests signed with the account key with 403. Only Microsoft Entra ID requests, plus user delegation SAS where applicable, are accepted.

The portal sets MinimumTlsVersion to TLS 1.2 by default. PowerShell, Azure CLI and ARM templates leave the property unset, so it returns no value until you configure it explicitly. TLS 1.3 can be negotiated but can't be set as the minimum.

Setting AllowBlobPublicAccess to false overrides the anonymous access setting of every container in the account. The $web static website container is unaffected and always public. Containers default to no public read access (Private).
Owner, Contributor and Storage Account Contributor can change these account settings, and all three include listkeys/action, which gives full data access through the account keys.
Infrastructure encryption (double encryption) has to be enabled when the account is created. Customer-managed keys can be stored in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM.
To protect a storage account with Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies, you must disallow Shared Key authorization on the account.

Azure Storage stopped supporting TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on February 3, 2026, for new and existing accounts; TLS 1.2 is now the effective minimum. Older guidance saying an unset account accepts TLS 1.0 predates this retirement.

Set TLS 1.2: az storage account update --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --min-tls-version TLS1_2
Disable Shared Key: az storage account update --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --allow-shared-key-access false
Verify: az storage account show --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --query "{tls:minimumTlsVersion, sharedKey:allowSharedKeyAccess, anon:allowBlobPublicAccess}"
Try listing containers with key auth: az storage container list --account-name <unique> --auth-mode key

objectives.summary: The storage firewall restricts the public endpoint with four kinds of rules: virtual network rules (which rely on service endpoints), public IP rules, resource instance rules, and the trusted Azure services exception. Exam questions focus on rule limits, the restrictions on IP rules, what each rule type actually grants, and how much precedence trusted services get.

keyFacts.fact: The four network rule types are virtual network rules, IP network rules, resource instance rules and trusted service exceptions. Each storage account supports up to 400 IP network rules and up to 400 virtual network rules.

IP rules accept public IPv4 addresses only. RFC 1918 private ranges aren't allowed, /31 and /32 prefixes have to be entered as single addresses, and IP rules have no effect on requests from the same Azure region as the account.

A resource instance rule opens the public endpoint to a specific Azure resource, which must be in the same tenant but can be in any subscription. It doesn't grant data access, so the resource's managed identity still needs an Azure role.

Microsoft recommends resource instance rules over the broad 'Allow Azure services on the trusted services list' exception because they create a smaller trust surface. The exception covers only documented service scenarios and doesn't open the account to all of Azure.

Trusted service access has the highest precedence. If you switch Public network access from 'selected networks' to Disabled, existing resource instance rules and exceptions, trusted services included, stay in effect.

Firewall rules apply only to data-plane operations, not control-plane operations. Enabling a service endpoint on a subnet switches its traffic to a private source IP, so IP rules for that subnet's old public IP stop working.

objectives.summary: Defender for Storage (the current plan, priced per storage account) has three parts. Activity monitoring is always on. Malware scanning is billed per GB, runs on upload or on demand, and is powered by Microsoft Defender Antivirus. Sensitive data threat detection is free with the plan. You need to know the defaults, the monthly scan cap, the ways scan results are delivered and their prerequisites, and how to override subscription-level settings for one account.

keyFacts.fact: Enabling the plan at subscription level in the portal turns on on-upload malware scanning and sensitive data threat detection by default. Sensitive data threat detection adds no cost, while malware scanning is billed per GB scanned.

On-upload scanning has a default cap of 10,000 GB (10 TB) per storage account per month. Scanning stops once the cap is reached, give or take about 20 GB, and the cap resets at midnight UTC at the end of each month.

Scan results go to blob index tags (on by default, but not tamper-resistant) and to Defender for Cloud alerts. You can also send them to an Event Grid custom topic for near-real-time automation, which must be in the same region as the storage account, allow public network access and use the Event Grid schema. A Log Analytics workspace stores them in the StorageMalwareScanningResults table.
The built-in 'soft delete malicious blobs' remediation is off by default. If blob soft delete isn't already on, turning the feature on enables it, with a default retention of 7 days (range 1–365).

To give one storage account settings that differ from the subscription, such as its own Event Grid topic or a different cap, set 'Override Defender for Storage subscription-level settings' to On for that account.

Sensitive data threat detection runs an agentless sampling engine that uses Microsoft Purview sensitive information types. Results usually arrive within 24 hours, new accounts are scanned within 6 hours, and rescans happen weekly.
Defender for Cloud raises an alert when an account reaches 75% of its monthly scan cap and another when the cap is reached and scanning stops for the rest of the month.
On-upload malware scanning requires the Microsoft.EventGrid resource provider to be registered, and enabling it creates an Event Grid system topic in the storage account's resource group.

objectives.summary: Delegated access to Azure Storage relies on shared access signatures. A user delegation SAS is signed with Entra credentials, and a service SAS or account SAS is signed with the account key. A stored access policy gives you server-side control and a way to revoke service SAS tokens. The exam tests which SAS types can use stored access policies, how to revoke each type, the limits (five policies and seven days), and the least-privileged role needed to create a user delegation SAS.

keyFacts.fact: There are three SAS types. A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key from Microsoft Entra ID and is the type Microsoft recommends. A service SAS covers one storage service and is signed with the account key. An account SAS covers one or more services, including service-level operations, and is also signed with the account key.

Stored access policies work only with a service SAS. A user delegation SAS or account SAS must be an ad hoc SAS. Blob containers, file shares, queues and tables each support up to five stored access policies, and a sixth returns 400 (Bad Request).

A start time, expiry time or permission can be set on the SAS token or on the stored access policy, not on both. A new or changed policy can take up to 30 seconds to take effect, and requests may get 403 in the meantime.

To revoke a service SAS tied to a stored access policy, delete the policy, change its expiry to the past, or rename its identifier. Recreating a policy under the same name revives old tokens. An ad hoc service or account SAS can be revoked only by regenerating the account key that signed it.

A user delegation key, and so any SAS it signs, is valid for at most 7 days. Revoking the user delegation keys (az storage account revoke-delegation-keys) invalidates every SAS they signed, though caching can delay the effect.

Requesting a user delegation key needs generateUserDelegationKey at storage account, resource group or subscription scope. The least-privileged built-in role is Storage Blob Delegator, which you can add for a principal whose data role is scoped only to a container.

Open the SAS URL in a browser to confirm the download works.
Return to Access policy and delete policy-read (or rename its identifier), then save. Wait about 30 seconds.
Open the same SAS URL again.

objectives.summary: Platform-level security for Azure SQL covers who can authenticate (Microsoft Entra-only authentication), how data at rest is protected (TDE with service-managed or customer-managed keys), and which networks can reach the logical server (IP firewall rules, virtual network rules, private endpoints, and the Public network access switch). Exam questions focus on role boundaries, prerequisites that cause a setup to fail, and what each network control actually blocks.

keyFacts.fact: Turning on Microsoft Entra-only authentication disables SQL authentication for the whole logical server or managed instance; existing SQL logins are not deleted, they simply can no longer connect. A Microsoft Entra admin must be set first or the setting stays unavailable.

SQL Security Manager can toggle Microsoft Entra-only authentication but can't set or remove the Microsoft Entra admin. SQL Server Contributor can set the admin but can't toggle the setting, and SQL Managed Instance Contributor can't toggle it either. A role such as Contributor holds both permissions.

For customer-managed TDE, the key vault (or Managed HSM) must have soft delete and purge protection enabled, otherwise TDE protector setup fails. The server identity needs get, wrapKey and unwrapKey (or the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role under Azure RBAC).

If the server loses access to the customer-managed TDE protector, databases become inaccessible after 30 minutes. If access is restored within 30 minutes the database self-heals within the next hour; after that, extra recovery steps are needed.

Server-level IP firewall rules apply to every database on the server and are stored in master; database-level IP firewall rules can be created only with T-SQL (sp_set_database_firewall_rule) and only after a first server-level rule exists.

Allow Azure services and resources to access this server adds a 0.0.0.0 rule that admits any Azure resource, including resources in other customers' subscriptions. Setting Public network access to Disable allows only private endpoint connections and blocks edits to firewall rules (error 42101).

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > SQL servers > (server) > Settings > Microsoft Entra ID (Support only Microsoft Entra authentication); Security > Networking (Public access / Private access); Security > Transparent data encryption

In Cloud Shell, set yourself as Microsoft Entra admin: az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv, then az sql server ad-admin create -g RG-Sql1 -s sqlcontoso01 --display-name <your UPN> --object-id <id>.
Enable Entra-only authentication: az sql server ad-only-auth enable -g RG-Sql1 -n sqlcontoso01, then confirm with az sql server ad-only-auth get -g RG-Sql1 -n sqlcontoso01.

In the portal open the server > Security > Networking > Public access, choose Selected networks, select Add your client IPv4 address, and make sure Allow Azure services and resources to access this server is unchecked. Save.
Connect with the Query editor using SqlAdmin1 (SQL auth) and note the failure; connect again with Microsoft Entra authentication and run SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('IsExternalAuthenticationOnly').

Set public network access to Disabled: az sql server update -g RG-Sql1 -n sqlcontoso01 --set publicNetworkAccess=Disabled, then try to add a firewall rule in the portal and observe that it is refused.
