questions.scenario: Fabrikam enables Microsoft Entra-only authentication on logical server SQL2, which already has a SQL login named AppLogin1. The server is also configured for customer-managed TDE with a key in KV1.
questions.question: For each statement, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: AppLogin1 is deleted from the server when Microsoft Entra-only authentication is enabled.
A Microsoft Entra user with the right permissions can still create new SQL logins, but those logins cannot connect.
If SQL2 loses access to the key in KV1 for 20 minutes and access is then restored, the databases heal automatically without extra recovery steps.

questions.explanation: Enabling Entra-only authentication does not remove existing SQL logins; it only stops them connecting, so statement 1 is false. Entra principals can still create SQL logins and users, but new ones cannot connect either, so statement 2 is true. With customer-managed TDE the database goes inaccessible after 30 minutes without key access; if access returns within 30 minutes, it heals automatically within the next hour, so statement 3 is true.

questions.scenario: Contoso has logical server SQL3. Requirements: (1) only clients in VNet1 may connect, via a private IP; (2) a security team must block any future attempt to add public IP firewall rules; (3) Azure resources in other tenants must never be able to reach the server.
questions.question: Select the configuration that meets each requirement.

dropdowns.label: Private connectivity from VNet1
options: A virtual network service endpoint rule
A server-level IP firewall rule for VNet1's address range

dropdowns.label: Block changes to public firewall rules
options: Set Public network access to Disable

dropdowns.label: Stop access from other tenants' Azure resources
options: Leave Allow Azure services and resources to access this server enabled
Turn off Allow Azure services and resources to access this server

questions.explanation: A private endpoint gives the server a private IP inside VNet1; a service endpoint still targets the public endpoint, and an IP firewall rule for private addresses does not create private connectivity. Setting Public network access to Disable allows only private endpoint traffic and rejects firewall rule changes (error 42101); minimum TLS and removing database rules do neither. The Allow Azure services option adds a 0.0.0.0 rule admitting any Azure resource regardless of subscription, so it must be off; Entra-only auth controls authentication, not network reachability.

objectives.summary: Azure SQL Database auditing is configured as a server policy or a database policy and writes to Azure Storage, Log Analytics, Event Hubs, or any combination. Azure SQL Managed Instance instead uses SQL Server Audit created with T-SQL, writing to a blob URL or to EXTERNAL_MONITOR through a diagnostic setting. Typical traps are double auditing, the hidden diagnostic setting, and which targets MI supports.

keyFacts.fact: A server auditing policy applies to every existing and newly created database on the server and always applies, whatever the database setting says. Enabling database auditing as well does not override it; the database is audited twice in parallel.
Microsoft recommends server-level auditing only, and adding database-level auditing only when one database needs a different destination, retention, or event set.

The default audit policy uses BATCH_COMPLETED_GROUP, SUCCESSFUL_DATABASE_AUTHENTICATION_GROUP and FAILED_DATABASE_AUTHENTICATION_GROUP, which capture all queries, stored procedures, and successful and failed logins.
Auditing to Log Analytics or Event Hubs creates a diagnostic setting named SQLSecurityAuditEvents_xxxx. Deleting it makes auditing fail silently, so Microsoft suggests alerting on its deletion.
In SQL Managed Instance, SQL Audit works at the server level and supports only the URL (Azure Blob storage) or EXTERNAL_MONITOR targets; TO FILE and Windows logs are not supported.
Failed logins that use Microsoft Entra authentication don't appear in the SQL audit log because the request never reaches the database; review them in Microsoft Entra sign-in logs instead.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > SQL servers > (server) > Security > Auditing (server policy); SQL databases > (database) > Security > Auditing (database policy); SQL managed instances > (instance) > Monitoring > Diagnostic settings (SQLSecurityAuditEvents)

lab.title: Enable server-level auditing to Log Analytics and query the events
steps: Create a Log Analytics workspace LAW-Audit1 in the same region as an existing logical server and database (for example sqlcontoso01/DB1 from the previous lab).
In the portal open SQL servers > sqlcontoso01 > Security > Auditing, set Enable Azure SQL Auditing to On, select Log Analytics, choose LAW-Audit1 and Save.
Open SQL databases > DB1 > Security > Auditing and confirm that database-level auditing is Off (the server policy already covers it).
Open sqlcontoso01 > Monitoring > Diagnostic settings (on the master database) and note the auto-created SQLSecurityAuditEvents_ setting; do not delete it.
Run a few queries against DB1 with the Query editor, wait about 10 minutes, then in LAW-Audit1 run: AzureDiagnostics | where Category == 'SQLSecurityAuditEvents' | take 50.
Optional: in the database Auditing blade select View audit logs to see the same events.
lab.verify: The KQL query returns BATCH_COMPLETED and authentication events for DB1 even though only the server policy is enabled.

flashcards.front: Server auditing is on and you also enable database auditing on DB1. What happens?
flashcards.back: Both policies run side by side and DB1 is audited twice. The database policy does not override the server policy.

flashcards.front: Which two audit targets does SQL Managed Instance support in CREATE SERVER AUDIT?
flashcards.back: TO URL (Azure Blob storage) and TO EXTERNAL_MONITOR (Event Hubs or Azure Monitor logs through a diagnostic setting). TO FILE isn't supported.

flashcards.front: What breaks SQL auditing to Log Analytics without any error?
flashcards.back: Deleting the auto-created diagnostic setting SQLSecurityAuditEvents_xxxx. Auditing then fails silently.

questions.scenario: Contoso has server-level auditing enabled on SQL1 to StorageAcct1. The compliance team asks for table-insert events from database Payroll only, stored in a separate Log Analytics workspace, without duplicating events for other databases.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Disable server auditing and enable database auditing on every database
Enable database-level auditing on Payroll with a custom action group targeting the Log Analytics workspace
Change the server audit policy to target the Log Analytics workspace
Create a diagnostic setting on Payroll for the SQLInsights category
questions.explanation: Microsoft recommends server auditing everywhere and adding database auditing only when a single database needs different event types or a different destination, which is exactly this case. Disabling server auditing and configuring every database adds overhead and risks gaps. Changing the server policy would send all databases to the new workspace. SQLInsights is a performance diagnostic category, not security auditing.

sources.title: Auditing policy at the server and database level

questions.scenario: You need SQL Managed Instance MI1 to send audit events to a Log Analytics workspace.
questions.question: Put the actions in the correct order.
items: On MI1, add a diagnostic setting that sends the SQLSecurityAuditEvents category to the Log Analytics workspace
Connect to MI1 and run CREATE SERVER AUDIT [Audit1] TO EXTERNAL_MONITOR
Create and enable a server audit specification or database audit specification for Audit1
Run ALTER SERVER AUDIT [Audit1] WITH (STATE = ON)
questions.explanation: Learn's procedure for MI is: create the diagnostic setting with SQLSecurityAuditEvents first, create the server audit TO EXTERNAL_MONITOR, create the audit specification(s), and finally turn the server audit on. Without the diagnostic setting, EXTERNAL_MONITOR has nowhere to deliver events. Server-level portal auditing (the Azure SQL Database method) is not how MI auditing works.

Failed Entra sign-ins never reach the database, so they appear in Microsoft Entra sign-in logs, not the SQL audit log.

objectives.summary: Defender for Databases in Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a bundle of four separately priced plans: Azure SQL Databases, SQL Servers on Machines, Open-Source Relational Databases, and Azure Cosmos DB. Turning on the Databases plan at subscription level turns on all four. Know which engines and APIs each plan covers and what Defender for SQL adds (vulnerability assessment and Advanced Threat Protection).

keyFacts.fact: Turning the Databases plan On under Defender for Cloud > Environment settings enables all four database plans and protects every supported database in the subscription; each plan is billed separately.

Defender for Open-Source Relational Databases protects Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server and Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server (all pricing tiers), plus AWS RDS Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. It isn't supported on Azure Arc-enabled machines.
Defender for Azure Cosmos DB supports only the API for NoSQL; Cassandra, MongoDB, Table and Gremlin APIs aren't supported. It doesn't read account data and doesn't affect performance.
Cosmos DB alerts cover potential SQL injection, anomalous access (for example Tor exit nodes or suspicious IPs) and suspicious activity such as unusual account key listing.

Microsoft Defender for SQL bundles SQL vulnerability assessment and Advanced Threat Protection for Azure SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance. Enabling or managing it needs SQL Security Manager or a database/server admin role.

When the Defender for Azure SQL plan is enabled, Defender for Cloud turns on Advanced Threat Protection and vulnerability assessment with the express configuration, which doesn't need a customer storage account.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > (subscription) > Defender plans > Databases > Select types

lab.title: Enable Defender for Databases and generate sample alerts
steps: In a trial subscription open Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings and select the subscription.

On the Defender plans page, set Databases to On, then select Select types and review the four plans (Azure SQL Databases, SQL servers on machines, Open-source relational databases, Azure Cosmos DB). Save.
Open an existing logical server (or create one) > Security > Microsoft Defender for Cloud and confirm that vulnerability assessment shows the express configuration.
Back in Defender for Cloud, open Security alerts > Sample alerts, select the subscription and the Azure SQL Databases and Azure Cosmos DB plans, and select Create sample alerts.
After a few minutes, open the generated alerts and review the description, MITRE tactic and recommended actions.
Set the Databases plan back to Off if you don't want charges after the trial.
lab.verify: Sample alerts for SQL and Cosmos DB appear on the Security alerts page, and the SQL server shows Defender for SQL as enabled.

questions.question: Why is this alert treated as potentially high impact even though its listed severity is only Informational?
options: Account keys only allow reading metadata, so the alert is informational
An extracted account key gives full control over the account's databases and data

objectives.summary: Network security groups (NSGs) filter traffic to and from subnets and network interfaces using prioritized, stateful 5-tuple rules. Application security groups (ASGs) let you write those rules against workload roles instead of IP addresses. Expect questions on priority ranges, default rules, subnet plus NIC evaluation order, and ASG virtual network constraints.

keyFacts.fact: Custom NSG rule priority ranges from 100 to 4096; lower numbers are processed first and processing stops at the first match. Default rules sit at 65000-65500 and can't be deleted, only overridden.

NSGs are stateful: if outbound traffic on a port is allowed, the return traffic is allowed automatically without an inbound rule. Removing a rule affects only new connections; existing flows keep working.

Default inbound rules allow VirtualNetwork-to-VirtualNetwork (65000) and AzureLoadBalancer (65001), then DenyAllInbound (65500). The VirtualNetwork tag also includes peered VNets and on-premises address space reached through gateways.
When an NSG is on both a subnet and a NIC, inbound traffic is evaluated by the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG; outbound is NIC first then subnet. Traffic must be allowed by both.
All NICs in an ASG must be in the same virtual network as the first NIC added to it. If a rule uses ASGs as both source and destination, both ASGs' NICs must be in the same VNet.
A single NSG rule can't list multiple service tags, but augmented rules can combine multiple IP addresses, ranges and ports in one rule.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Network security groups > (NSG) > Settings > Inbound security rules / Outbound security rules / Subnets / Network interfaces; Application security groups > Create

lab.title: Segment a web and database tier with ASGs
steps: Create resource group RG-Nsg1 and VNet1 (10.0.0.0/16) with subnet App (10.0.1.0/24).
Create two ASGs: az network asg create -g RG-Nsg1 -n AsgWeb and az network asg create -g RG-Nsg1 -n AsgDb.
Create two small Linux VMs (VMWeb1 and VMDb1) in subnet App with no public IP, and in each VM's Networking > Application security groups, add VMWeb1's NIC to AsgWeb and VMDb1's NIC to AsgDb.
Create NSG1 and associate it with subnet App: az network nsg create -g RG-Nsg1 -n NSG1; az network vnet subnet update -g RG-Nsg1 --vnet-name VNet1 -n App --nsg NSG1.

Add rule Allow-Web-To-Db (priority 110): az network nsg rule create -g RG-Nsg1 --nsg-name NSG1 -n Allow-Web-To-Db --priority 110 --source-asgs AsgWeb --destination-asgs AsgDb --destination-port-ranges 1433 --protocol Tcp --access Allow.
Add rule Deny-All-To-Db (priority 120) with source * and destination AsgDb on port 1433, access Deny.
Open VMDb1 > Networking > Network settings > the NIC > Effective security rules and confirm both rules appear above AllowVnetInBound.
lab.verify: Effective security rules for VMDb1 show Allow-Web-To-Db (110) and Deny-All-To-Db (120) before the default 65000 rule.

flashcards.front: Valid priority range for custom NSG rules
flashcards.back: 100 to 4096. Lower number = higher priority. Default rules use 65000, 65001 and 65500.

flashcards.front: Evaluation order for inbound traffic when NSGs exist on both the subnet and the NIC
flashcards.back: Subnet NSG first, then NIC NSG. Outbound is the reverse: NIC first, then subnet.

flashcards.front: Can an ASG contain NICs from two different virtual networks?
flashcards.back: No. Every NIC must be in the same VNet as the first NIC assigned to the ASG.

questions.scenario: Contoso has AsgLogic, containing NICs in VNet1, and AsgDb, containing NICs in VNet2. VNet1 and VNet2 are peered. Admin1 tries to create an NSG rule with source AsgLogic and destination AsgDb, and the operation fails.
questions.question: What is the cause?
options: The NICs in both ASGs used in one rule must be in the same virtual network
ASGs can be used only as a destination, never as a source
The rule priority must be above 4096 for ASG rules
questions.explanation: When ASGs are used as both source and destination in the same rule, all their NICs must exist in the same VNet; peering doesn't change that. NSGs work fine on peered VNets. ASGs can be used as source or destination. The custom priority range is 100-4096; there is no special range for ASG rules.

questions.scenario: VM1 has an NSG on its subnet (NSG-Sub) and on its NIC (NSG-Nic). NSG-Sub allows inbound TCP 443 from Internet. NSG-Nic has only default rules. An admin removes an inbound SSH allow rule while a user has an active SSH session.
questions.question: For each statement, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: Inbound HTTPS from the internet reaches VM1.
The active SSH session is disconnected immediately when the rule is removed.
Outbound traffic from VM1 is evaluated by NSG-Nic before NSG-Sub.

questions.explanation: Inbound traffic must pass both NSGs. NSG-Nic has only default rules, and AllowVNetInBound doesn't cover internet sources, so DenyAllInbound blocks it; statement 1 is false. NSG rule changes affect only new connections, so the existing SSH session continues; statement 2 is false. Outbound traffic hits the NIC NSG first, then the subnet NSG; statement 3 is true.

questions.explanation: Custom priorities run from 100 (highest) to 4096 (lowest); 1 is the top of the AVNM security admin range, not NSGs. objectives.summary: Azure Virtual Network Manager (AVNM) lets a central team push security admin rules to whole network groups of VNets across subscriptions. These rules are evaluated before NSGs, and their action type decides whether NSGs still get a say. Know the three actions, the priority range, the one-configuration-per-region limit, and which services skip admin rules.

keyFacts.fact: Security admin rules are evaluated before NSG rules. Allow passes traffic on to NSG evaluation, while Always Allow and Deny end evaluation: Always Allow delivers traffic and bypasses NSGs, and Deny drops it.
Security admin rule priority is 1-4096, lower number = higher priority. Protocols include TCP, UDP, ICMP, ESP, AH or Any.
Only one security admin configuration can be deployed per region; to get more policy sets in a region, add rule collections to that configuration.
Security admin rules apply at the virtual network level, are deployed with eventual consistency, and automatically protect new resources added to in-scope VNets.

By default, admin rules skip VNets containing SQL Managed Instance or Azure Databricks; with AllowRulesOnly, only Allow rules apply there. They also skip subnets with services such as Azure Firewall, Bastion, VPN Gateway and Application Gateway without network isolation.
Security admin rules don't support the AzurePlatformDNS, AzurePlatformIMDS and AzurePlatformLKM service tags.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Virtual Network Manager > Network managers > (instance) > Settings > Configurations > Create > Security admin configuration > Rule collections; then select the configuration > Deploy

lab.title: Block inbound RDP across a network group with a security admin rule
steps: Create two VNets (VNet-A, VNet-B) in the same region in resource group RG-Avnm1.
Create a network manager: portal > Virtual Network Manager > Create, scope = your subscription, features = Security admin.
Under Network groups, create NG-Prod and add VNet-A and VNet-B as static members.
Under Configurations, select Create > Security admin configuration named SAC1, add rule collection RC-Baseline targeting NG-Prod.
Add rule Deny-RDP: Priority 10, Action Deny, Direction Inbound, Protocol TCP, Source * , Destination port 3389. Save and create.
Select SAC1 > Deploy, choose the region of the VNets, and deploy.
Create a VM in VNet-A with an NSG that allows RDP (3389) from Any, then run Network Watcher > IP flow verify for inbound TCP 3389.
lab.verify: IP flow verify returns Access denied and names the AVNM security admin rule, even though the NSG allows RDP.

flashcards.front: Which AVNM security admin actions stop traffic from being evaluated by NSGs?
flashcards.back: Always Allow (delivers the traffic) and Deny (drops it). Allow continues on to NSG evaluation.

flashcards.front: How many security admin configurations can be deployed to one region?
flashcards.back: One. Use multiple rule collections inside that configuration for more rule sets.

flashcards.front: Priority range for AVNM security admin rules
flashcards.back: 1 to 4096 (lower is higher priority).

questions.scenario: Contoso's network team must guarantee that monitoring traffic on TCP 5986 from 10.50.0.0/24 always reaches every VM in 40 spoke VNets, even if an application team adds an NSG rule that denies it.
questions.question: Which security admin rule action should you use?
questions.explanation: Always Allow ends evaluation and delivers the traffic directly, bypassing conflicting NSG rules. Allow passes the traffic on to NSG evaluation, so an app team's deny NSG rule could still block it. Deny does the opposite of what's needed. An NSG rule is controlled per subnet or NIC and can be changed by app teams, so it doesn't give a central guarantee.

objectives.summary: A Virtual WAN hub becomes a secured virtual hub when Azure Firewall (or a supported NVA or SaaS solution) is deployed in it and managed by Azure Firewall Manager policy. Routing intent with Internet and Private traffic routing policies sends traffic through that security solution without hand-built UDRs. The key traps are inter-hub inspection, default route propagation, and custom route tables.

keyFacts.fact: A secured virtual hub is a Virtual WAN hub with security and routing policies configured by Azure Firewall Manager; it gives automated routing so you don't build UDRs to steer traffic to the firewall. Routing intent must be configured to secure inter-hub and branch-to-branch traffic, even within a single hub.
Routing intent is the only Virtual WAN mechanism for inspecting inter-hub traffic with security appliances in the hub, and it must be enabled on all hubs so traffic is routed symmetrically.

Each hub supports at most one Internet traffic routing policy and one Private traffic routing policy, each with a single next hop. The Internet policy advertises 0.0.0.0/0 to connections; that default route doesn't propagate across hubs.
Virtual WANs that use custom route tables and customized policies can't be used with routing intent constructs.
When you configure routing intent through Azure Firewall Manager, only next hop resources of type Azure Firewall are supported.

Firewall Policy is a global resource that can be associated with firewalls in secured virtual hubs and hub virtual networks across regions and subscriptions; classic rules protect virtual networks only.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Firewall Manager > Virtual hubs > (hub) > Settings > Security configuration (Internet traffic / Private traffic, Inter-hub); Firewall Manager > Azure Firewall Policies

lab.title: Build a secured virtual hub with routing intent
steps: Create a spoke VNet Spoke-01 (10.0.0.0/16) in resource group RG-Vwan1.
Open Firewall Manager > Virtual hubs > Create new secured virtual hub; create a new Virtual WAN, hub address space 10.100.0.0/23, and include Azure Firewall (Standard or Basic tier to save cost).
In the Virtual WAN, add a Virtual network connection from the hub to Spoke-01.
In Firewall Manager > Azure Firewall Policies, create Policy-01 with a network rule collection that allows TCP 22 and 80 between spokes, then associate it with the hub's firewall.
Open Firewall Manager > Virtual hubs > the hub > Security configuration. Set Internet traffic to Azure Firewall and Private traffic to Azure Firewall, set Inter-hub to Enabled, and save.
In the Virtual WAN hub, open Effective Routes for the Spoke-01 connection and confirm 0.0.0.0/0 and the private prefixes point to the Azure Firewall.
Delete RG-Vwan1 when done (secured hubs incur hourly charges).
lab.verify: Effective routes show the hub firewall as next hop for internet and private prefixes, and firewall logs show spoke traffic being processed.

flashcards.front: What turns a Virtual WAN hub into a secured virtual hub?
flashcards.back: Deploying a security solution such as Azure Firewall in the hub, with security and routing policies managed by Azure Firewall Manager.

flashcards.front: What must be configured to inspect inter-hub and branch-to-branch traffic in Virtual WAN?

flashcards.front: Does the 0.0.0.0/0 route from an Internet traffic routing policy propagate to other hubs?
flashcards.back: No. Internet traffic must egress through the local hub's security solution.

questions.scenario: Contoso has Hub1 (secured, Azure Firewall) and Hub2 (regular, no firewall) in one Virtual WAN. Hub1 has Internet and Private routing policies. Users in VNets connected to Hub2 report they can't reach the internet through Hub1's firewall.
questions.question: Why?
options: Hub2 VNets need a UDR pointing to Hub1's firewall
The default route advertised by Hub1's Internet policy doesn't propagate across hubs
Azure Firewall in a hub supports only private traffic
Routing intent requires custom route tables on Hub2
questions.explanation: Routing intent advertises 0.0.0.0/0 only to connections of the local hub; it doesn't propagate across hubs, so Hub2's VNets can't use Hub1's firewall for internet. UDRs on spokes aren't the Virtual WAN mechanism here. Azure Firewall in a hub can handle internet traffic. Routing intent can't be used with custom route tables at all.

questions.question: Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.

Configure a Private traffic routing policy on HubWest

objectives.summary: VPN security in Azure is about choosing cryptography and authentication. Site-to-site and VNet-to-VNet connections can use a custom per-connection IPsec/IKE policy instead of the defaults. Point-to-site connections authenticate users with certificates, Microsoft Entra ID, or RADIUS, and each method only works with certain tunnel types.

keyFacts.fact: Custom IPsec/IKE policies are supported on all VPN Gateway SKUs except Basic. Only one policy combination is allowed per connection, and you must specify every IKE and IPsec parameter; partial policies aren't allowed.

After a custom IPsec/IKE policy is set, the Azure gateway sends and accepts only that exact proposal on the connection, so the on-premises device must match or the tunnel won't come up. SA lifetimes are local and don't need to match.
If you use GCMAES for IPsec encryption, you must use the same GCMAES algorithm and key length for IPsec integrity (for example GCMAES256 for both).
The IKE main mode SA lifetime is fixed at 28,800 seconds on Azure VPN gateways; the quick mode SA lifetime defaults to 27,000 seconds and 102,400,000 KB.
P2S authentication types are Certificate, Microsoft Entra ID, and RADIUS. Microsoft Entra ID authentication works only with the OpenVPN tunnel type; SSTP and IKEv2 support only certificate or RADIUS.

For certificate P2S you upload the trusted root certificate's public key to the gateway, and every client needs a client certificate generated from that root. The Basic gateway SKU doesn't support IKEv2 or RADIUS.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Virtual network gateways > (gateway) > Settings > Point-to-site configuration; Connections > (S2S connection) > Settings > Configuration > IPsec / IKE policy: Custom

lab.title: Apply a custom IPsec/IKE policy to a site-to-site connection
steps: Create VNet1 with a GatewaySubnet and deploy a route-based VPN gateway VNet1GW (VpnGw1 SKU; deployment takes 30-45 minutes).
Create local network gateway Site6 with a placeholder public IP (for example 203.0.113.10) and address space 10.61.0.0/16.
Create connection VNet1toSite6 (type Site-to-site IPsec, IKEv2, shared key abc123) between VNet1GW and Site6.
Open the connection > Configuration, select IPsec / IKE policy = Custom, and set IKE Phase 1: AES256 / SHA384 / DHGroup24; IKE Phase 2: AES256 / SHA256 / PFS None; SA lifetime 27000 seconds. Save.

Alternatively run: az network vpn-connection ipsec-policy add -g <rg> --connection-name VNet1toSite6 --ike-encryption AES256 --ike-integrity SHA384 --dh-group DHGroup24 --ipsec-encryption AES256 --ipsec-integrity SHA256 --pfs-group None --sa-lifetime 27000 --sa-max-size 102400000.
Run az network vpn-connection ipsec-policy list -g <rg> --connection-name VNet1toSite6 to confirm, then delete the resources to stop gateway charges.
lab.verify: The connection's Configuration page and the ipsec-policy list output both show the custom algorithms.

objectives.summary: Microsoft Entra Private Access is the Zero Trust Network Access part of Global Secure Access. It replaces VPNs by tunneling traffic from the Global Secure Access client through Microsoft's edge to private network connectors, with Conditional Access per app. Quick Access is the broad starting point and per-app Global Secure Access apps give finer segmentation.

keyFacts.fact: Private Access lets you define private FQDNs and IP addresses; users with the Global Secure Access client reach them without a VPN, and access is controlled with Conditional Access.

Quick Access is the primary group of FQDNs and IP ranges you always tunnel; Global Secure Access (per-app) apps let you apply different Conditional Access policies to subsets of resources. Microsoft positions Quick Access as a transition step toward per-app access.

Quick Access setup order: create a connector group with at least one active private network connector, configure Quick Access, assign users and groups, configure Conditional Access, and enable the Private Access traffic forwarding profile.
Private network connectors run on Windows Server 2016 or later, need only outbound ports 80 and 443 (no inbound ports), and TLS inspection or termination of their outbound traffic should be avoided.
Users must be assigned directly or through a group to the Quick Access app; nested groups aren't supported.
Configuring Quick Access needs the Global Secure Access Administrator and Application Administrator roles; managing connector groups needs Application Administrator and Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2.

lab.title: Publish an internal file share with Quick Access
steps: Prerequisites: a tenant with Entra ID P1 plus Private Access (trial), a Windows Server 2016+ VM with line of sight to a test SMB share, and an Entra-joined Windows 11 test device.
On the server, sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center, go to Global Secure Access > Connect > Connectors, download and install the connector service, and register it. Confirm it shows Active.
Create a connector group (for example CG-Lab) containing the connector.

Go to Global Secure Access > Applications > Quick access, name the app, select CG-Lab, then under Network access properties add an application segment for the file server IP with port 445, protocol TCP. Save.
On the Quick Access app, select Users and groups and assign a test user directly (nested groups aren't supported).
Go to Global Secure Access > Connect > Traffic forwarding and enable the Private access profile for the test user.
Install the Global Secure Access client on the Windows 11 device, sign in as the test user, and open \\<fileserver IP>\share.
lab.verify: The share opens from outside the network with no VPN, and the Global Secure Access client's Advanced diagnostics > Traffic tab shows the SMB flow tunneled through Private Access.

objectives.summary: A private endpoint is a NIC with a private IP in your VNet that maps to one specific PaaS resource and subresource. Clients keep using the normal FQDN, and DNS (usually an Azure Private DNS zone named privatelink.<service>) points it to the private IP. A private endpoint doesn't block public access by itself, and NSG/UDR policies on the endpoint subnet are off by default.

keyFacts.fact: Azure creates a public CNAME from the service FQDN to the privatelink zone, so connection strings don't change; a linked Private DNS zone (for example privatelink.database.windows.net for SQL Database) returns the private IP. Auto-creation of zone records works only with the recommended zone names.

Each subresource needs its own private endpoint and zone, for example blob uses privatelink.blob.core.windows.net and file uses privatelink.file.core.windows.net. Don't put records for different services in the same zone.
Creating a private endpoint doesn't block the resource's public endpoint; you must also disable public network access (for Azure SQL, set Public network access to Disable).

Network policies for private endpoints are disabled on subnets by default, so NSGs and UDRs don't apply to private endpoint traffic until you enable them (NSG only, route tables only, or both). The setting affects all private endpoints in the subnet.
A private endpoint injects a /32 route; to force traffic through a firewall, a UDR must use a prefix equal to or more specific than the VNet address space, so a 0.0.0.0/0 UDR doesn't override it.
A successful public DNS lookup of a privatelink CNAME doesn't grant access; if public access is disabled the service still rejects public connections.

From your own PC run the same nslookup (public IP returned) and try to list containers; note that access is denied because public access is disabled.

objectives.summary: Azure Private Link service lets you publish your own service, running behind a Standard Load Balancer, so consumers in other VNets, subscriptions or tenants reach it through private endpoints. You control who can see it (visibility), who is auto-approved, and you approve or reject the rest. Consumer traffic is source-NATed from a NAT IP in your VNet.

keyFacts.fact: Private Link service attaches to the frontend IP configuration of a Standard Load Balancer; Basic Load Balancer isn't supported, and backend pools configured by IP address aren't supported (NIC-based only). Private Link Service Direct Connect, which skips the load balancer, is in preview.
Azure generates a globally unique alias (Prefix.GUID.region.azure.privatelinkservice) that you share with consumers; they connect using the alias or the resource ID.

Visibility controls who can discover and request a connection (RBAC only, restricted by subscription, or anyone with the alias). Auto-approval is a subset of visibility; requests from visible but not auto-approved subscriptions stay Pending until the provider approves.
Consumer traffic arrives with a NAT IP from the provider's subnet as its source. To see the real consumer IP and private endpoint LinkID, enable TCP Proxy v2 and make the app parse the header.
The subnet hosting the Private Link service NAT IPs must have privateLinkServiceNetworkPolicies disabled; the portal does this automatically, but CLI, PowerShell and templates need an extra step.
Private Link service supports IPv4, TCP and UDP only, must be in the same region as its VNet and load balancer, supports up to eight NAT IPs, and has an idle timeout of about 5 minutes.

Note the alias with az network private-link-service show -g RG-Pls1 -n pls1 --query alias.
In a separate VNet-Consumer, create a private endpoint using Connect to an Azure resource by resource ID or alias and paste the alias.
Back on pls1 > Private endpoint connections, approve the Pending request, then browse to the endpoint's private IP from a VM in VNet-Consumer.

objectives.summary: Azure Firewall is a stateful, managed firewall available as Basic, Standard and Premium. It processes rules in a fixed type order (DNAT, network, application) on top of group and collection priority, with threat intelligence evaluated first. Know which features need DNS proxy or Premium, and how SNI/Host header matching works for application rules.

keyFacts.fact: Azure Firewall always processes DNAT rules, then network rules, then application rules, regardless of rule collection group or collection priority. Within each type it processes groups and collections by priority (100-65,000), and parent policy groups always win over child policy groups.

Rules are terminating: a network rule match stops processing, so application rules aren't checked. Application rules apply to HTTP, HTTPS and MSSQL; HTTP matches on Host header and HTTPS on SNI only (without TLS inspection). Application rules aren't applied to inbound connections (use WAF), and changing a rule to deny drops existing sessions.

Using FQDNs in network rules requires DNS proxy on the firewall, and clients should use the firewall's private IP as their DNS server. With DNS proxy on, the firewall listens on port 53 and forwards to Azure DNS or your custom DNS.

Basic is limited to about 250 Mbps, threat intel alert mode only, no DNS proxy, no network-rule FQDN filtering and no web categories. Standard adds threat intel deny, DNS proxy, network FQDN filtering and web categories. Premium adds TLS inspection, IDPS, URL filtering and full-URL web categories.

Premium TLS inspection uses an intermediate CA certificate stored in Azure Key Vault. A user-assigned managed identity reads it through the Key Vault Secrets interface, so it needs Get and List secret permissions (not certificate permissions).
IDPS in Alert mode runs in parallel with rule processing; in Alert and Deny mode it runs inline after the rules engine and drops matching sessions silently (no TCP RST).

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Firewall Policies > (policy) > Settings > DNS (Proxy), TLS inspection, IDPS, Threat Intelligence; Rule collections (DNAT / Network / Application); Firewalls > (firewall) > Firewall Manager / Firewall policy

lab.title: Deploy Azure Firewall with DNS proxy and test rule ordering
steps: Create RG-Fw1 and VNet-Fw (10.0.0.0/16) with AzureFirewallSubnet (10.0.1.0/26) and Workload (10.0.2.0/24). Deploy Azure Firewall Standard FW1 with a new firewall policy FWP1 and a public IP.
Create route table RT-Workload with route 0.0.0.0/0 > Virtual appliance > FW1 private IP, and associate it with Workload.
In FWP1 > DNS, enable DNS Proxy. In VNet-Fw > DNS servers select Custom and enter FW1's private IP; restart the workload VM so it picks up the setting.
In FWP1 add an application rule collection (priority 200, Allow) with rule Allow-MS: source 10.0.2.0/24, protocol https:443, target FQDN www.microsoft.com.
Add a network rule collection (priority 300, Allow) with rule Allow-Web: source 10.0.2.0/24, destination *, TCP 80,443.

From the workload VM browse to www.bing.com: it succeeds because the network rule is processed before application rules. Then delete Allow-Web and retry: www.bing.com is now denied and www.microsoft.com still works.
Optionally send firewall diagnostics to a Log Analytics workspace to review the rule hits, then delete RG-Fw1.
lab.verify: With the network rule present, all HTTPS sites load; after removing it, only www.microsoft.com loads and other FQDNs are denied.

objectives.summary: Network Watcher diagnostics answer 'why is this traffic allowed or blocked?'. IP flow verify tests one TCP/UDP flow against NSG and AVNM admin rules for a VM, NSG diagnostics extends that to ICMP, prefixes, service tags and scale sets, and Effective security rules shows the merged rule set on a NIC. Flow logs record actual traffic; virtual network flow logs replace NSG flow logs, which are retiring.

keyFacts.fact: IP flow verify checks whether a packet is allowed or denied for a VM's NIC, considering NSGs on the subnet and NIC plus Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules, and returns the name of the rule that decided it.
IP flow verify tests only TCP and UDP and only VM NICs; for ICMP or virtual machine scale sets, use NSG diagnostics. A Network Watcher instance must exist in the VM's subscription and region.

NSG diagnostics works for VMs, scale sets and application gateways, accepts an IP address, IP prefix or service tag, reports the deciding rule, and lets you add a new higher-priority rule to change the result.
Effective security rules shows every rule applied to a NIC: the NIC NSG, the subnet NSG, and the aggregate of both, including default rules. It can be downloaded as CSV for audits.

NSG flow logs retire on September 30, 2027 and new NSG flow logs can no longer be created; virtual network flow logs are the replacement and also record AVNM security admin decisions and encryption status.

The flow log storage account must be in the same region as the VNet (or NSG), must be Standard tier (premium isn't supported), and can be in another subscription in the same Entra tenant. Private endpoint traffic is captured at the source VM, not at the endpoint.

objectives.summary: Before rolling out Microsoft Copilot and agents, you need to find SharePoint and OneDrive content that is shared too broadly, because Copilot surfaces anything a user can already reach. SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM) provides data access governance (DAG) reports, AI insights, site access reviews, restricted access control (RAC) and Restricted Content Discovery (RCD). Together they let you identify oversharing and either reduce discoverability or tighten access.

keyFacts.fact: Data access governance reports are found in the SharePoint admin center under Reports > Data access governance and help identify sites with potentially overshared or sensitive content. Snapshot reports and activity reports (for example sharing links created in the last 28 days) are available.

DAG report types include permission state reports for sites/OneDrive/files, site permissions for a given user, sensitivity label snapshot, sharing links activity, and Everyone except external users (EEEU) insights; reports can also be generated with SharePoint Online PowerShell (Start-SPODataAccessGovernanceInsight).

Restricted Content Discovery is a site-level setting that stops a site's content from appearing in organization-wide search and Copilot responses; it does not change permissions and users with access can still open content directly. It applies to SharePoint sites only, not OneDrive.

RCD can be enabled in the SharePoint admin center (Active sites > site > Settings) or with Set-SPOSite -Identity <url> -RestrictContentOrgWideSearch $true. Index propagation can take a long time; sites with more than 500,000 items can take over a week.

Remediation options after a DAG report include restricted access control (limit a site to a specific group), reviewing the Change history report, and initiating a site access review so site owners update permissions.

Review the sites with the most Anyone or organization-wide links and pick a test site (for example 'Contoso HR Test').
Go to Sites > Active sites, select the test site, open the Settings tab and turn Restrict content discovery (Restrict content from Microsoft Copilot) On, then Save.
Optionally run in SharePoint Online PowerShell: Get-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/hrtest | Select RestrictContentOrgWideSearch

objectives.summary: Microsoft Purview Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) for AI gives a central place to see AI activity, sensitive data in prompts and responses, and oversharing risk for Copilot, agents and third-party AI apps. A classic DSPM for AI experience still exists, while a newer unified Data Security Posture Management adds objectives, AI observability and Security Copilot agents. Key tools are one-click policies, data risk assessments, Activity explorer and recommendations.

keyFacts.fact: DSPM for AI automatically runs a weekly default data risk assessment for the top 100 SharePoint sites by usage; custom data risk assessments (preview) can target specific users or sites.
DSPM for AI offers one-click preconfigured policies; allow at least 24 hours for new policies to collect data. Using it requires permissions such as the Microsoft Entra Compliance Administrator role.

From a data risk assessment's Protect tab you can restrict access by label (DLP policy that stops Copilot summarizing labeled data), restrict all items with SharePoint Restricted Content Discovery, create an auto-labeling policy, or create retention policies.
Activity explorer shows AI interactions (prompts and responses), sensitive information types and AI website visits, grouped into Copilot experiences and agents, Enterprise AI apps, and Other AI apps.

The newer Data Security Posture Management adds data security objectives (such as preventing data exposure in Copilot interactions) and AI observability, an inventory of AI apps and agents with activity in the last 30 days.

objectives.summary: Copilot Studio custom agents can call an external threat detection system at runtime before each tool invocation, and Microsoft Defender can act as that system. When real-time protection is enabled, Defender scans tool invocations, blocks suspicious actions such as cross-prompt injection, and raises alerts. Setup is a joint task between a Security Administrator in the Defender portal and a Power Platform administrator. The Copilot Studio side of the feature is documented as preview.

keyFacts.fact: In the Defender portal go to Settings > Security for AI > Get started, select the Copilot Studio step and toggle Real-time protection on; then share the provided URL with the Power Platform administrator and paste back the Entra App ID.

The Power Platform administrator configures it in Power Platform admin center > Security > Threat detection > Additional threat detection, selecting the environment, allowing data sharing, entering the Entra App ID and the endpoint link (preview).
If the threat detection system does not answer within one second, the agent allows the tool call by default; Set error behavior can be changed to Block the query.
External threat detection is only called for generative agents that use generative orchestration; classic agents are skipped.
If the Microsoft 365 connector is not connected, real-time protection still blocks suspicious Copilot Studio activity, but related alerts and incidents do not appear in the Defender portal.

Real-time protection uses a built-in Default rule that only audits, plus custom rules that block chosen detection types (secret exfiltration, malicious content propagation, evasion techniques, unsafe email domain) scoped to specific agents.

Paste the App ID into the Defender portal App ID field and select Save.
In Defender go to Settings > Security for AI > Policies & rules > Real-time protection and create a custom rule that blocks Secret exfiltration for a test agent.

objectives.summary: Conditional Access for agents extends the Conditional Access engine to Microsoft Entra Agent ID. You must target the right token subject: a user (on-behalf-of access), an agent identity or blueprint (app-only access), or an agent's user account. Policies can use agent risk from ID Protection (preview) and custom security attributes to scale. Agents can't satisfy interactive controls like MFA, so they need their own policies. Microsoft Entra Agent ID itself is documented as preview, and the agent user targeting options are labelled preview.

keyFacts.fact: Conditional Access for agents requires Microsoft 365 E7, or a Microsoft Agent 365 license paired with at least Microsoft Entra P1 or Microsoft 365 E3; creating policies needs the Conditional Access Administrator role.

Access patterns map to policy targets: on-behalf-of (delegated) targets users and groups; app-only targets an agent identity or agent identity blueprint; agent-user access targets the agent's user account. A policy for one subject doesn't apply to the others.
Policies scoped through the Users assignment, including All users, don't apply to agent user accounts; you must select Agents and then All agent users (preview) or specific agent users.

Targeting an agent identity blueprint covers every agent identity created from it, including future ones; custom security attributes let policies apply automatically to agents with matching attributes.

To block risky agents, include All agent identities, target All resources, set Conditions > Agent risk (preview) to High, grant Block, and start in Report-only mode. Agent risk-based policies additionally need Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft 365 E5 alongside Agent 365 (E7 covers both).
Conditional Access doesn't apply when an agent uses an API key instead of Entra tokens, or when security defaults are enabled.

Under Target resources include All resources.
Under Conditions > Agent risk (Preview) set Configure to Yes and select High.
Under Grant select Block, set Enable policy to Report-only, and select Create.

objectives.summary: Microsoft Defender XDR gives an AI agent inventory with risk levels and attack-surface relationships, and its incident graph includes blast radius analysis that shows possible paths from a compromised entity to critical targets. For agents managed through Microsoft Agent 365, Defender correlates agent alerts into incidents so analysts can trace root cause and blast radius. These agent detection capabilities and the blast radius graph are documented as preview, and Learn does not document a separate 'agent-only' blast radius tool beyond these experiences.

keyFacts.fact: Detection and investigation of threats to AI agents in Microsoft Defender is in public preview and covers agents managed through Microsoft Agent 365; analysts use the incident graph to see relationships between entities and the blast radius of AI agent threats.

Blast radius analysis in the incident graph (preview, in the legacy incident experience) is built on the Microsoft Sentinel data lake and graph, shows possible propagation paths from a selected node to predefined critical targets, and requires Sentinel data lake onboarding; Learn states it's available to customers who onboarded to the data lake before September 23, 2026.

In the incident graph, select a node and choose View blast radius; the view shows the top-rated attack paths, and path calculations are bounded to up to seven hops. Exposure management (read) permission or higher is needed.
Blast radius accuracy depends on available environment data; if critical assets aren't defined, the graph won't fully represent risk.

Assets > AI agents in the Defender portal shows each agent's risk level, risk indicators, recommendations, alerts, identity information and attack-surface relationships; the AgentsInfo Advanced Hunting table holds agent inventory data.

objectives.summary: Managing Entra Agent ID access means assigning accountable humans (owners and sponsors), granting least-privilege access through entitlement management access packages, and disabling agents or blueprints when needed. Owners are technical administrators; sponsors are accountable for lifecycle and access. Admins can disable individual agents, entire blueprints, or block agent authentication tenant-wide with Conditional Access. Microsoft Entra Agent ID is documented as preview.

keyFacts.fact: Sponsors are required when creating agent identities and blueprints; agent identity sponsors can be users or select groups (dynamic or Microsoft 365) with up to 100 sponsors, no more than 5 groups. They can disable or delete the agent and modify its sponsors.

Owners are optional, can be users or service principals (not groups), can edit authentication properties and credentials, and unlike sponsors can re-enable a disabled agent identity, restore soft-deleted identities, or hard-delete them.
Owners and sponsors manage their agents in the My Account portal (Manage agents) and request access packages for them in the My Access portal ('Requesting for Sponsored agent' or 'Owned agent').
If a sponsor leaves the organization, sponsorship automatically transfers to the sponsor's manager; Lifecycle Workflows provide mover and leaver tasks to notify managers and cosponsors.

Disable scopes: individual agent (admin center or My Account), blueprint level (blocks existing agent identities and creation of new ones), or tenant-wide with Conditional Access policies that block agent authentication. Agent ID Administrator can disable agents in Entra ID > Agents.
Access packages for agents can grant security group memberships, application OAuth API permissions (including Microsoft Graph application permissions) and Microsoft Entra roles.

objectives.summary: The AI gateway in Azure API Management governs traffic to language model APIs, MCP servers and agents. Key policies are llm-token-limit for TPM limits and quotas, semantic caching backed by Azure Managed Redis, and content safety checks using Azure AI Content Safety. You can import a Microsoft Foundry API with these policies preconfigured, or enable AI Gateway directly from the Foundry portal (the Foundry integration is preview).

keyFacts.fact: The llm-token-limit policy enforces tokens-per-minute limits or token quotas over hourly to yearly periods on any counter key (for example subscription ID or IP) and can precalculate prompt tokens to reject oversized requests before they reach the backend.

Semantic caching uses llm-semantic-cache-store and llm-semantic-cache-lookup with Azure Managed Redis or another RediSearch-compatible external cache and an Embeddings API to reuse completions for similar prompts.
When importing a Microsoft Foundry API, the wizard offers tabs for Manage token consumption, Apply semantic caching, and AI content safety (llm-content-safety policy) to block unsafe prompts.

AI gateway in Microsoft Foundry (preview): in the Foundry portal, Manage > AI Gateway > Add AI Gateway either creates a Basic v2 APIM instance or reuses an existing v2-tier instance in the same tenant and subscription; new projects are enabled by default but existing projects must be added manually.
A request exceeding the TPM limit returns 429 Too Many Requests; exceeding the total token quota returns 403 Forbidden. Limits apply at project level.
AI gateway content safety can enable Prompt Shields for jailbreak and prompt-injection detection and blocklists, and can start in log-only mode before blocking (AI Gateway tier, preview).

objectives.summary: Defender for AI Services is a Defender for Cloud plan that provides runtime threat protection for Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI workloads, working with Prompt Shields and Microsoft threat intelligence to alert on jailbreaks, data leakage and credential theft. You enable it per subscription on the Defender plans page and then choose components such as suspicious prompt evidence, data security for AI interactions (Purview, preview) and AI model security (preview). Alerts integrate with Defender XDR.

keyFacts.fact: Enable the plan in Azure portal > Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > subscription > Defender plans by toggling AI services On; Owner or Contributor level is needed.

Plan components include suspicious prompt evidence (GA), data security for AI interactions (preview; uses Microsoft Purview and is a paid Purview feature not included in the plan), and AI model security (preview) for models in Azure Machine Learning registries.
If user prompt evidence is disabled, Defender for Cloud still analyzes prompts and responses for threats but masks prompt content in alerts.

AI threat protection is generally available, includes a 30-day free trial capped at 75 billion tokens scanned, scans text tokens only, and isn't available for connected AWS accounts or Azure Government.
You can add end-user and application context parameters to Azure AI API calls so alerts identify the user or app behind a request.

objectives.summary: In Microsoft Foundry, a guardrail is a named collection of controls; each control defines a risk, the intervention points to scan and the action (annotate or annotate and block). Models support user input and output intervention points, while agents add tool call and tool response (preview). Prompt Shields detect user prompt attacks and document (indirect) attacks. Agent guardrails are in preview, and an agent's guardrail fully overrides its model's guardrail.

keyFacts.fact: Four intervention points exist: user input, tool call (preview, agents only), tool response (preview, agents only), and output.
Risks in an agent are detected based on the guardrail assigned to the agent, not its underlying model; the agentic guardrail fully overrides the model's guardrail.

Blocking levels for harm categories: Low blocks only high severity, Medium blocks medium and high, High blocks low, medium and high; turning output filtering off requires approval for modified guardrails.
User prompt attack detection is on by default; document attack detection is off by default and must be enabled. Document attacks can be scanned at the tool response point for agents (preview).

Microsoft Default guardrails such as Default.V2 can't be edited; create a custom guardrail. Violence, Hate, Sexual and Self-harm controls on inputs and outputs can only be overridden, not deleted. Creating guardrails needs Foundry Account Owner or higher.
A guardrail can also be specified per request with the x-policy-id header, which overrides the deployment-level configuration for that call.

lab.title: Create a custom guardrail with indirect attack protection for an agent
steps: With Foundry Account Owner on a test Foundry project that has a model deployment and an agent, open the Foundry portal and select Build > Guardrails > Create Guardrail.

Select the risk Document attack (indirect attack), choose the tool response intervention point, and action Annotate and block, then select Add control (Spotlighting isn't supported for agents, so leave it off).
Override the Violence control to the High blocking level on user input and output and confirm the override.
Select Next, Add agents, pick your test agent, and Save.
Name the guardrail 'Contoso-Agent-Guardrail' and select Create.
Select the guardrail row and choose Try in Playground to send test prompts.
lab.verify: When a blocking control triggers, the playground shows which risk was detected and at which intervention point; the agent lists the new guardrail under Guardrails.

objectives.summary: Azure managed disks offer several encryption layers. Server-side encryption (SSE) is always on and can use customer-managed keys through a disk encryption set. Encryption at host extends SSE to temp disks and caches end to end. Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) encrypts inside the guest with BitLocker or DM-Crypt and is scheduled to retire on 15 September 2028. Confidential disk encryption binds keys to a confidential VM's TPM. Know what each layer covers and when to choose it.

keyFacts.fact: SSE always encrypts OS and data disks at rest with 256-bit AES and can use customer-managed keys when configured with a disk encryption set (DES); it doesn't encrypt temp disks or disk caches.
Encryption at host encrypts temp disks and OS/data disk caches at rest and keeps data encrypted as it flows to storage; temp disks use only platform-managed keys, and it doesn't consume VM CPU.

Azure Disk Encryption is scheduled for retirement on 15 September 2028; after that, ADE-encrypted disks fail to unlock on reboot. Use encryption at host for new VMs or confidential VMs with OS disk encryption.

Encryption at host requires registering the EncryptionAtHost feature in the Microsoft.Compute namespace; enable it with az vm create --encryption-at-host or az vm update --set securityProfile.encryptionAtHost=true, and the VM must be deallocated to disable it.

For customer-managed keys, the Key Vault or Managed HSM must be in the same region as the disks and must have purge protection enabled; if the key is disabled, deleted or expired, VMs using it automatically shut down.
Confidential disk encryption binds disk encryption keys to the VM's TPM so protected content is accessible only to that VM; it applies to the OS disk, with temp disk encryption as an opt-in.

Run: az vm create -g rg-enc-lab -n vmEnc1 --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_D2s_v5 --encryption-at-host --generate-ssh-keys
Run: az vm show -g rg-enc-lab -n vmEnc1 --query securityProfile.encryptionAtHost -o tsv

Finally, the VM is created with encryption at host and the disk encryption set. Any other sequence fails because a dependency doesn't exist yet.

objectives.summary: Azure Bastion provides RDP and SSH to VMs over TLS on port 443 without public IPs on the VMs. Choosing the SKU is the key planning decision. Developer is free and supports one VM at a time with no peering. Basic gives two fixed instances. Standard adds native client, shareable links, IP-based connect, custom ports, file transfer and host scaling. Premium adds session recording and private-only deployment.

keyFacts.fact: Basic, Standard and Premium require a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet of /26 or larger; Developer uses shared infrastructure and needs neither the subnet nor a public IP.
Developer SKU supports one VM connection at a time and doesn't support virtual network peering; Basic has a fixed two instances (40 RDP / 80 SSH sessions).
Standard adds native client (Azure CLI) connections, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom inbound ports, file upload/download and host scaling from 2 to 50 instances.
Premium adds graphical session recording (stored in a blob container, authenticated with a SAS URL or a managed identity (preview)) and private-only deployment with no public IP.
Session recording isn't available through the native client, and recording storage must not use immutable storage policies or blob versioning.
SKU upgrades take about 10 minutes; downgrading isn't supported, so you must delete and recreate Bastion.

objectives.summary: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access is a Defender for Servers Plan 2 feature that keeps management ports closed with deny rules and opens them only on approved request, for a limited time and from specific source IPs. It works with NSGs and with Azure Firewall classic rules, and also supports AWS EC2 (preview). Users request access from Defender for Cloud, the VM's Connect page, PowerShell or REST.

keyFacts.fact: JIT requires Defender for Servers Plan 2 and supports Resource Manager VMs and VMs protected by Azure Firewall in the same VNet; classic VMs and firewalls managed by Azure Firewall Manager policies aren't supported.
Defender for Cloud recommends protecting ports 22 (SSH), 3389 (RDP), 5985 and 5986 (WinRM); for each port you set protocol, allowed source IPs and maximum request time.

When a request is approved, Defender for Cloud configures the NSG and Azure Firewall to allow the requested ports from the specified IP for the approved time; when it expires the NSG is restored, new connections are blocked and established connections aren't interrupted.
To request access a user needs Microsoft.Security/locations/jitNetworkAccessPolicies/initiate/action plus read permissions; Set-JitLeastPrivilegedRole script creates a least-privileged role.
PowerShell uses Set-AzJitNetworkAccessPolicy to configure JIT and Start-AzJitNetworkAccessPolicy to request access; a VM shows as Unsupported if it has no NSG or Azure Firewall.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Workload protections > Just-in-time VM access > Not configured / Configured

lab.title: Enable JIT on a VM and request access
steps: Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2 on a trial subscription containing a Windows VM with an NSG.
Open Defender for Cloud > Workload protections > Just-in-time VM access > Not configured, select the VM and choose Enable JIT on VMs.
Keep port 3389, set Allowed source IPs to Per request and Maximum request time to 1 hour, then Save.
Go to the Configured tab, select the VM and choose Request access; select port 3389, My IP, a 1-hour window, then Open ports.
Open the VM's NSG and review the inbound rules.
lab.verify: The NSG shows the JIT deny rule for 3389 plus a temporary allow rule for your IP while the request is active; after the window, the NSG returns to its previous state.

objectives.summary: Azure Arc-enabled servers project on-premises and other-cloud machines into Azure through the Connected Machine agent, so Defender for Cloud, Azure Policy and Machine Configuration can manage them. Arc also gives local security controls that only a local admin can change: extension allowlists and blocklists, monitor mode, and disabling the guest configuration agent or remote connectivity. These are important for Tier 0 servers such as domain controllers.

keyFacts.fact: Microsoft recommends onboarding non-Azure machines as Azure Arc-enabled servers so they get the full set of Defender for Servers features; the Arc Connected Machine agent is installed on them.

Extension allowlists and blocklists are set locally with azcmagent config set extensions.allowlist/blocklist; nobody in Azure, even an Owner or Global Administrator, can override them. Allowlists are preferred because they block new extensions by default.

Monitor mode (azcmagent config set config.mode monitor) applies a Microsoft-managed allowlist of monitoring and security extensions, disables remote connectivity and disables the machine configuration agent.

For Tier 0 assets, consider a dedicated subscription, disabling incoming connections (incomingconnections.enabled false), disabling guest configuration, and allowlisting only needed extensions such as AMA and MDE.Windows.
The Custom Script Extension and Run Command run as Local System or root; block them unless needed because attackers could use them to run malicious code.

Run: azcmagent config set guestconfiguration.enabled false
Run: azcmagent config list to review the settings.
From the Azure portal, try installing the Custom Script Extension on the machine.

objectives.summary: Agentless machine scanning takes snapshots of VM disks and analyzes them out of band, so no agent or network connectivity is needed and VM performance isn't affected. Defender for Cloud snapshots the OS and data disks, keeps the copy in the same region, analyzes it in an isolated scanning environment, and deletes the snapshot once metadata is collected (typically minutes).
In Azure, the built-in VM scanner operator role is used; scanning CMK-encrypted disks needs extra Key Vault key read, wrap and unwrap permissions.

Only machines that are running during a scheduled scan are scanned; allow up to 24 hours for results after enabling or changing permissions.

objectives.summary: Trusted Launch protects Generation 2 VMs against bootkits, rootkits and kernel malware with Secure Boot, a virtual TPM and boot integrity monitoring. It's selected through the VM's security type (Standard, Trusted launch, or Confidential). Trusted Launch is the default for new Gen2 VMs created in the portal, CLI and PowerShell. Integrity monitoring installs the Guest Attestation extension so Defender for Cloud can attest boot health and alert on failures.

keyFacts.fact: Secure Boot ensures only signed OS boot components (boot loader, kernel, kernel drivers) load; if an image isn't signed by a trusted publisher the VM fails to boot.
The vTPM is TPM 2.0 compliant, runs outside the VM's reach, measures the whole boot chain and enables remote attestation.

Boot integrity monitoring requires Secure Boot and vTPM plus the Guest Attestation extension; enable it in the portal at VM > Configuration > Security type > Integrity monitoring, or with --enable-integrity-monitoring in the CLI.

Defender for Cloud recommends enabling Secure Boot, vTPM and the Guest Attestation extension, and raises a medium-severity alert when VM attestation fails; attestation fails if Secure Boot is disabled.
Create a Trusted Launch VM with az vm create --security-type TrustedLaunch --enable-secure-boot true --enable-vtpm true; updating Secure Boot or vTPM on an existing VM triggers a reboot.
Trusted Launch doesn't increase VM pricing; Managed Image and Linux VM hibernation aren't supported, and Gen1 VMs can be upgraded to Gen2 Trusted Launch.

objectives.summary: Azure Machine Configuration (formerly guest configuration) audits and optionally enforces settings inside Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers, delivered through Azure Policy. Azure VMs need the Machine Configuration extension and a system-assigned managed identity, which the 'Deploy prerequisites to enable Guest Configuration policies on virtual machines' initiative deploys at scale. Arc servers already include the agent. Assignment types control whether settings are only audited, applied once and monitored, or automatically corrected.

keyFacts.fact: Azure VMs need the machine configuration extension and a system-assigned managed identity; Arc-enabled servers don't need the extension because it's included in the Connected Machine agent.

Assign the initiative 'Deploy prerequisites to enable Guest Configuration policies on virtual machines' to a management group, subscription or resource group to deploy the extension and identity at scale.

Assignment types: Audit (report only), ApplyAndMonitor (apply once, then report drift without correcting), ApplyAndAutoCorrect (apply and correct drift at the next evaluation). The property is case sensitive.
Configurations that change machines use the DeployIfNotExists effect; selecting Create a remediation task during assignment applies the configuration to existing noncompliant machines.
The machine configuration agent can't exceed 5% CPU, for both built-in and custom definitions, and the same limit applies to the service in the Arc Connected Machine agent.
Machine Configuration supports up to 50 guest assignments per machine, and per-setting results appear on the Guest assignments page.
Defender for Servers Plan 2 uses the Machine Configuration extension to assess OS configuration against Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark compute baselines.

objectives.summary: Defender for Containers protects Kubernetes clusters, nodes, workloads, registries and images across AKS, EKS, GKE and Arc-enabled clusters. It combines agentless capabilities (Kubernetes API discovery, control plane posture, registry and running-image vulnerability assessment, control plane threat detection) with sensor-based capabilities (the eBPF Defender sensor DaemonSet for runtime threat detection, antimalware, DNS detection and binary drift). Exam questions usually hinge on which capability needs an in-cluster component and which plan or component toggle turns it on.

keyFacts.fact: Image vulnerability assessment, Kubernetes posture assessment and control plane threat detection are agentless; runtime threat detection requires in-cluster components (the Defender sensor).

On AKS the Defender sensor is a lightweight DaemonSet that uses eBPF to collect process, network and Kubernetes event telemetry; it is deployed as an AKS Security profile and needs only outbound HTTPS 443, with no inbound connections to the cluster.

Agentless discovery for Kubernetes creates an identity, assigns it the built-in Kubernetes Agentless Operator role at subscription scope, and uses AKS Trusted Access to bind a ClusterRole that gives Defender read access to the data plane. It can be enabled from either Defender CSPM or Defender for Containers.

The Containers plan settings expose separate components: Agentless scanning for machines, Defender sensor (with optional Security Gating and Runtime Anti Malware), Azure Policy, Kubernetes API access, and Registry access (with Security findings). Registry vulnerability assessment requires Registry access to be enabled.

New or imported registry images are typically scanned within a few hours, and a daily rescan covers images pushed or pulled in the last 30 days or currently running in monitored clusters; older unused images stop getting updated findings until pulled again.
Gated deployment uses vulnerability findings to audit or deny deployments of images that do not meet your vulnerability policy before they are admitted to the cluster.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > <subscription> > Defender plans > Containers > Settings

lab.title: Enable Defender for Containers components on a trial subscription
steps: Sign in to the Azure portal and open Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings.
Select your trial subscription, find the Containers row on the Defender plans page and set it to On.
Select Settings on the Containers row and turn on Defender sensor, Azure Policy, Kubernetes API access and Registry access. Select Continue, then Save.
Create a small AKS cluster (az aks create -g rg-lab -n aks-lab --node-count 1 --generate-ssh-keys) and an ACR, then push or import any public image into the registry.
Run kubectl get pods -n kube-system and look for microsoft-defender-collector and microsoft-defender-publisher pods.
After a few hours, open Defender for Cloud > Recommendations and search for the registry image vulnerability recommendation.
lab.verify: Defender sensor pods are Running in kube-system, and the recommendation for Azure registry container images with vulnerabilities shows your registry once scanning completes.

flashcards.back: Runtime threat detection. Image vulnerability assessment and posture assessment are agentless.

flashcards.front: What technology does the Defender sensor DaemonSet use to collect runtime telemetry?
flashcards.back: eBPF, collecting Kubernetes events, process and network data from each node.

flashcards.back: Registry access (with the Security findings sub-option to link findings to images).

questions.scenario: Contoso has the Defender for Containers plan enabled on Sub1. Only the Kubernetes API access and Registry access components are turned on. AKS1 in Sub1 is running. questions.explanation: Runtime threat detection is not agentless; it needs the Defender sensor DaemonSet that collects process and network telemetry with eBPF. Azure Policy deploys Gatekeeper for posture and enforcement, not runtime detection. Agentless scanning for machines takes disk snapshots for vulnerabilities and secrets, which is out-of-band and does not see live processes. Security findings only links registry vulnerability results to images.

An image that was pushed 90 days ago, has not been pulled since, and is not running in any monitored cluster is still rescanned every day.

questions.explanation: Agentless discovery creates either a DefenderCSPMSecurityOperator or a DefenderForContainersSecurityOperator identity depending on which plan enabled it, so statement 1 is true. All Defender components use outbound-only connectivity (the publisher pod needs HTTPS 443 egress), so no inbound rule is needed. questions.scenario: Fabrikam has Defender for Containers enabled on Sub1, and Registry access with Security findings is already turned on. questions.question: Which two components should be enabled? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.
options: Defender sensor with Defender Security Gating enabled
Azure Policy for Kubernetes (Azure Policy component)
questions.explanation: Gated deployment needs the Defender sensor with Security Gating (plus Registry access with Security findings, which is already on); its admission controller audits or denies images that break your vulnerability rules. The Azure Policy add-on extends Gatekeeper v3 as an admission webhook, so a policy such as no privileged containers can be enforced and future requests blocked. Agentless machine scanning only assesses node disk snapshots and blocks nothing. Runtime Anti Malware detects (and can block) malicious file execution in running workloads, not deployments at admission. Note: Defender's Kubernetes misconfiguration enforcement, which relies on Kubernetes API access, is another documented way to block privileged containers.

objectives.summary: Securing AKS covers control plane identity (Microsoft Entra authentication, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization, disabling local accounts), control plane network exposure (authorized IP ranges or a private cluster), workload governance with the Azure Policy add-on, pod-to-Azure identity with Microsoft Entra Workload ID, and east-west traffic control with network policies. Watch for mutually exclusive options and the commands that implement each one.

keyFacts.fact: Local accounts are enabled by default, and the --admin credential stays a non-auditable back door even with Entra integration. Use az aks update --disable-local-accounts; on an existing cluster, rotate cluster certificates afterward to revoke credentials already issued.

With Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization, assign built-in roles such as Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader, Writer, Admin or Cluster Admin at cluster or namespace scope. RBAC Reader cannot read Secrets, and RBAC Writer can read Secrets and run pods as any service account in the namespace.
API server authorized IP ranges need the Standard load balancer SKU, allow up to 200 ranges, and cannot be used with private clusters.
A private cluster (--enable-private-cluster) exposes the API server only through a private endpoint in the VNet; --disable-public-fqdn also removes the publicly resolvable DNS name.

Workload identity requires the OIDC issuer and workload identity to be enabled on AKS Standard, a federated identity credential linking the managed identity to system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>, and the pod label azure.workload.identity/use: "true". A managed identity supports at most 20 federated credentials.

AKS network policy engines are Cilium (recommended, Linux, with FQDN and L7 policy support), Azure NPM and Calico (the option for Windows nodes). By default, all pods can talk to each other until a network policy is applied.

objectives.portalPath: Kubernetes services > <cluster> > Settings > Security configuration (authentication and authorization) / Networking (API server access) / Policies

lab.title: Harden an AKS cluster with Entra ID, Azure RBAC, authorized IPs and the Azure Policy add-on
steps: Create a Microsoft Entra group named aks-admins and note its object ID.

Create a cluster: az aks create -g rg-lab -n aks-sec --enable-aad --aad-admin-group-object-ids <groupId> --enable-azure-rbac --disable-local-accounts --enable-oidc-issuer --enable-workload-identity --network-plugin azure --network-dataplane cilium --generate-ssh-keys
Restrict API access: az aks update -g rg-lab -n aks-sec --api-server-authorized-ip-ranges <your-public-ip>/32
Register the provider (az provider register --namespace Microsoft.PolicyInsights) and run az aks enable-addons --addons azure-policy -g rg-lab -n aks-sec
Assign a user the Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader role at the cluster scope with az role assignment create.
Run az aks get-credentials --admin -g rg-lab -n aks-sec and confirm that it fails.
lab.verify: The --admin credential request returns a "disable local accounts" error, kubectl get pods -n gatekeeper-system shows Gatekeeper pods, and the RBAC Reader user can list pods but not secrets.

Requirement 2
Requirement 3

A private cluster or a disabled public FQDN changes network reachability, not authentication. --enable-azure-rbac makes Azure role assignments authorize Kubernetes API calls; the Policy add-on and network policy are unrelated to authorization. The configuration is not supported because authorized IP ranges cannot be used with private clusters
