questions.scenario: You must let the payments pod in namespace pay on AKS5 (AKS Standard) read a Key Vault secret by using Microsoft Entra Workload ID.
questions.question: Put the steps in the correct order.
items: Enable the OIDC issuer and workload identity on the cluster
Create a user-assigned managed identity and grant it access to the Key Vault
Create a Kubernetes service account annotated with the identity client ID
Create a federated identity credential using the cluster OIDC issuer URL and subject system:serviceaccount:pay:<sa-name>
Deploy the pod with the service account and the label azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
questions.explanation: This follows the documented Learn sequence. On AKS Standard the cluster must expose an OIDC issuer before Entra ID can trust its tokens. The managed identity must exist before you can annotate the service account with its client ID, and it needs Key Vault Secrets User (or equivalent) to read the secret. The federated credential ties the cluster issuer and the service account subject to the identity. Only then does deploying the labeled pod cause the webhook to inject the projected token.

objectives.summary: Azure Container Registry security covers authentication (prefer Microsoft Entra identities, keep the admin account off, use repository-scoped tokens and scope maps only for non-Entra clients), network isolation (private endpoints and disabling public access, IP rules, trusted services bypass), and image vulnerability scanning by Defender for Cloud. Tier requirements (Premium for networking) and side effects of disabling public access are common exam traps.

keyFacts.fact: The admin user is disabled by default, has full push and pull rights, and all its users appear as one identity. Built-in Azure Policy can audit, deny or modify registries to keep the local admin account disabled.

Repository-scoped tokens are tied to exactly one scope map that lists repositories and actions (content/read, content/write, content/delete, metadata/read, metadata/write). They work in all tiers but cannot be assigned to Entra identities.

Private endpoints need the Premium tier (up to 200 per registry). After you disable public network access, az acr build stops working unless you use dedicated agent pools or allow the task service tag IPs.
Public IP network rules are Premium-only, are capped at 200 rules, and do not apply to traffic arriving through private endpoints.
When public access is disabled, trusted services such as Microsoft Defender for Cloud can reach the registry only if the trusted services bypass setting is enabled.
Defender for Cloud surfaces registry findings as the recommendation "Azure registry container images should have vulnerabilities resolved (powered by Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management)".

objectives.portalPath: Container registries > <registry> > Settings > Access keys / Networking; Repository permissions > Tokens / Scope maps

lab.title: Lock down a Premium registry and issue a scoped token
steps: Create a Premium registry: az acr create -g rg-lab -n <acrname> --sku Premium
Confirm admin is off: az acr update -n <acrname> --admin-enabled false
Create a scoped token: az acr token create --name ci-pull --registry <acrname> --repository samples/hello-world content/read
Generate a password with an expiry: az acr token credential generate --name ci-pull --registry <acrname> --expiration-in-days 30 --password1
In the portal, add a private endpoint under Networking > Private access, then set Public network access to Disabled.
Under Networking, enable the setting that allows trusted Microsoft services to access the registry.
lab.verify: docker login with the token succeeds from a VM inside the VNet. A docker push to samples/hello-world fails because the token has read-only access, and access from the public internet is refused.

objectives.summary: For Azure Container Instances, the key controls are managed identity (including identity-based image pulls from ACR) and deploying container groups into a delegated VNet subnet. For Azure Container Apps, the controls are environment accessibility (external or internal), app ingress visibility, IP ingress restrictions, built-in authentication and managed identity image pulls. Several limitations, such as user-assigned only for ACI ACR pulls and no mixing of allow and deny rules, are classic distractors.

keyFacts.fact: ACI does not support system-assigned managed identity for ACR image pulls; you must use a user-assigned identity. A private-endpoint ACR must sit on a different subnet from the ACI-delegated subnet.
Container groups in a VNet must use a NAT gateway for outbound connectivity and cannot be exposed directly with a public IP or DNS label.
Container Apps IP restrictions are either all Allow or all Deny rules, which cannot be mixed. With no rules, all inbound traffic is allowed, and blocked clients receive "RBAC: Access Denied".
An internal Container Apps environment has no public endpoint, and this cannot be changed after creation. Private endpoints on an environment require public network access to be Disabled.
On an internal environment, "Limited to Container Apps Environment" ingress hides the app from the rest of the VNet as well; VNet clients receive HTTP 404 through the internal load balancer.
Container Apps can pull from ACR with a system-assigned or user-assigned identity, but Learn recommends user-assigned where possible. The identity needs the AcrPull role.

objectives.portalPath: Container App > Networking > Ingress (IP Restrictions); Container App > Settings > Identity; Container instances > Create > Networking (Private)

lab.title: Restrict Container Apps ingress and pull with a user-assigned identity
steps: Create a user-assigned identity: az identity create -g rg-lab -n uai-pull, then assign it AcrPull on your ACR.

Create a Container App that uses it: az containerapp create -n app1 -g rg-lab --environment env1 --user-assigned <ID> --registry-identity <ID> --registry-server <acr>.azurecr.io --image <acr>.azurecr.io/hello:latest --ingress external --target-port 80
Add an allow rule: az containerapp ingress access-restriction set -n app1 -g rg-lab --rule-name office --ip-address <your-ip>/32 --action Allow
Browse to the app URL from your IP, then from a phone on mobile data.
Run az containerapp ingress access-restriction list to review the rules.
lab.verify: The app loads from your IP, and requests from other IPs return RBAC: Access Denied.

objectives.summary: Function app security combines HTTP authorization levels and access keys, positive client authentication with App Service Authentication (Easy Auth) or APIM, inbound network controls (access restrictions, private endpoints) and outbound VNet integration, plus managed identity and Key Vault references for secrets. Hosting plan support for networking features is heavily tested.

keyFacts.fact: HTTP trigger authorization levels are anonymous (no key), function (function or host key), and admin (master key). The master key also grants admin access to runtime REST APIs and must not be distributed.
Access keys are shared secrets; Learn states that only positive client authentication, such as App Service Authentication, APIM or network isolation, truly secures endpoints.

Inbound access restrictions work on all hosting plans. Private endpoints are supported on Flex Consumption, Elastic Premium and Dedicated, but not on the Consumption plan, which also lacks outbound VNet integration.
VNet integration only affects outbound traffic. It does not give private inbound access; use a private endpoint for that.

Key Vault references use @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) or @Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=...;SecretName=...). They use the system-assigned identity by default, or keyVaultReferenceIdentity for a user-assigned one, which needs Key Vault Secrets User or Get permission on secrets.
Setting functionsRuntimeAdminIsolationEnabled to true disables the /admin endpoints, which otherwise accept the master key.

objectives.portalPath: Function App > Settings > Authentication; Settings > Networking > Inbound traffic configuration; Settings > Identity; Settings > Environment variables

lab.title: Require Entra sign-in and use a Key Vault reference in a function app
steps: Create a function app on a Flex Consumption or Premium plan in the portal.
Under Settings > Identity, turn on the system-assigned identity and save.
In your Key Vault (RBAC model), assign the function identity the Key Vault Secrets User role and create a secret named DbPassword.
Under Environment variables, add the app setting DbPassword = @Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=<vault>;SecretName=DbPassword) and apply it.
Under Settings > Authentication, add the Microsoft identity provider and require authentication with HTTP 401 for unauthenticated requests.
Under Networking > Public network access, choose Enabled from select virtual networks and IP addresses and add an Allow rule for your IP.

objectives.summary: Logic Apps security covers who can call request-based triggers (SAS, OAuth 2.0 with Microsoft Entra ID authorization policies, Easy Auth on Standard, inbound IP restrictions, APIM fronting), how workflows authenticate outbound (managed identities), and hiding sensitive data in run history with secure inputs and outputs and content IP restrictions. Consumption and Standard differ in where settings live.

keyFacts.fact: Consumption request triggers accept either SAS or OAuth 2.0 with Microsoft Entra ID per call, not both at once. You can disable SAS so that only OAuth is accepted.
An Entra authorization policy (type AAD, or AADPOP for Proof-of-Possession) must include at least the Issuer (iss) and Audience (aud) claims; each claim value is a single string.

Standard workflows starting with the Request trigger can use Easy Auth, the App Service built-in authentication, with a managed identity. Inbound IP rules for Standard are set under Networking > Access restrictions.

Secure Inputs and Secure Outputs hide values in run history (runtimeConfiguration.secureData.properties). Restricting content access to 0.0.0.0-0.0.0.0 blocks everyone from viewing run history inputs and outputs.

A Consumption logic app can use the system-assigned identity or a single user-assigned identity; a Standard logic app can have the system-assigned identity and multiple user-assigned identities enabled at once.

In the portal for Consumption apps, the Allowed inbound IP addresses option "Only other Logic Apps" allows only nested calls through the built-in Azure Logic Apps action; calls made with the HTTP action get 401.

objectives.portalPath: Logic app (Consumption) > Settings > Workflow settings > Access control configuration; Settings > Authorization; Logic app (Standard) > Settings > Networking > Access restrictions

lab.title: Restrict a Consumption logic app trigger to OAuth and hide secrets in run history
steps: Create a Consumption logic app with a When an HTTP request is received trigger and an HTTP action.
Under Settings > Authorization, add a policy of type AAD with claims Issuer = https://sts.windows.net/<tenantId>/ and Audience = the expected audience for your logic app resource.
In the trigger code view, set operationOptions to IncludeAuthorizationHeadersInOutputs and add the trigger condition @startsWith(triggerOutputs()?['headers']?['Authorization'], 'Bearer').
On the HTTP action, open Settings > Security and turn on Secure Inputs and Secure Outputs.
Under Workflow settings > Access control configuration, set the trigger access option to Specific IP ranges and enter your IP range.
Call the trigger with a bearer token from az account get-access-token, then open the run in run history.
lab.verify: Calls without a bearer token show the trigger as Skipped or fail, and the HTTP action inputs and outputs appear hidden in run history.

objectives.summary: App Service hardening includes transport security (HTTPS Only redirect, minimum inbound TLS for the site and the SCM site separately), inbound network filtering (access restrictions with priorities, service tags, HTTP header filters and an implicit deny), built-in authentication (Easy Auth), and managed identities for outbound access without secrets. Remember that private endpoint traffic bypasses access restrictions.

keyFacts.fact: The default minimum inbound TLS version for new apps is 1.2, and TLS 1.3 is supported. The site and the SCM (Kudu) site have independent minimum TLS settings, and deployment slots have their own.
HTTPS Only redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS. Because TLS terminates at the App Service load balancers, the app receives HTTP and can check the X-Forwarded-Proto header.

Access restriction rules are evaluated in priority order (lowest number first). When at least one rule exists and the unmatched action is not set, an implicit deny all applies. Blocked requests get HTTP 403, and an app can have up to 512 rules.
To accept traffic only from your own Front Door profile, allow the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and add an HTTP header filter on X-Azure-FDID with your profile ID.
Access restrictions apply only to inbound traffic through the default (public) endpoint; traffic arriving through a private endpoint is not evaluated against them.
An app can have one system-assigned identity, deleted with the app, and multiple user-assigned identities that can be shared across resources. Managed identity configuration is per deployment slot.

objectives.portalPath: App Service > Settings > Configuration > General settings (HTTPS Only, Minimum Inbound TLS Version); Settings > Networking > Public network access > Access restrictions; Settings > Authentication; Settings > Identity

lab.title: Enforce HTTPS and TLS 1.2+ and lock an app to Azure Front Door
steps: Create a web app: az webapp create -g rg-lab -p plan-lab -n <app> --runtime "NODE:20-lts"
Turn on HTTPS Only and set the minimum TLS: az webapp update -g rg-lab -n <app> --https-only true and az webapp config set -g rg-lab -n <app> --min-tls-version 1.2
Check both TLS settings: az webapp show -g rg-lab -n <app> --query "siteConfig.{siteTls:minTlsVersion, scmTls:scmMinTlsVersion}"
Get your Front Door ID: az afd profile show -g rg-lab --profile-name <afd> --query frontDoorId
Add the rule: az webapp config access-restriction add -g rg-lab -n <app> --priority 100 --service-tag AzureFrontDoor.Backend --http-header x-azure-fdid=<id>
Turn on the system-assigned identity: az webapp identity assign -g rg-lab -n <app>
lab.verify: http:// requests redirect to https://, direct browsing to <app>.azurewebsites.net returns 403, and the same app loads through the Front Door endpoint.

questions.scenario: WebApp2 has these access restriction rules and no unmatched rule action is configured: Allow 10.1.0.0/16 priority 300; Deny 10.1.5.0/24 priority 100; Allow 192.0.2.10/32 priority 200.
questions.question: Arrange the rules in the order App Service evaluates them, followed by the final behavior.
items: Deny 10.1.5.0/24 (priority 100)
Allow 192.0.2.10/32 (priority 200)
Allow 10.1.0.0/16 (priority 300)
Implicit deny all for unmatched traffic
questions.explanation: Rules are evaluated from the lowest priority number. A request from 10.1.5.20 is denied by the priority 100 rule before the broader allow is reached. Because rules exist and no unmatched action is set, anything that matches no rule is denied.

objectives.summary: Azure WAF runs on Application Gateway v2 and Azure Front Door through WAF policies. You need to know the modes (Detection logs only and is the default, Prevention blocks), Microsoft-managed rule sets (DRS 2.x and CRS 3.2) with anomaly scoring, custom rules (evaluated first; match or rate-limit; geo and IP filters), and tuning through exclusions, per-rule actions and exceptions. Tier support (Front Door managed rules need Premium or Classic) is a common trap.

keyFacts.fact: Detection mode logs threats without blocking; Prevention mode blocks and returns 403. Learn recommends running a new WAF in Detection first to tune exclusions and custom rules.

With CRS or DRS 2.1 and later, anomaly scoring is used: Critical=5, Error=4, Warning=3, Notice=2, and a score of 5 or more blocks in Prevention mode. The final block shows as rule 949110, while the contributing rules show "Matched".

Custom rules are processed before managed rules, ordered by priority (a lower number runs first). A matching Allow custom rule skips DRS, CRS and Bot Manager evaluation but is still evaluated by the HTTP DDoS ruleset (preview).

Exclusions remove a specific request attribute (for example, a header carrying Entra tokens) from inspection while the rest of the request is still evaluated. On Application Gateway they can be global or per rule.

On Front Door, managed rule sets are supported only in Premium and Front Door (classic). Custom rules, including rate limiting over a one-minute or five-minute window and geo-filtering, are available in Standard and Premium.
Front Door exclusions can be scoped to a rule set, a rule group or a single rule, and Learn recommends per-rule exclusions to keep them as narrow as possible.

objectives.portalPath: Web Application Firewall policies > <policy> > Policy settings (mode) / Managed rules / Custom rules / Exclusions

lab.title: Create a Front Door WAF policy with a rate-limit custom rule
steps: In the portal, create a Web Application Firewall policy for Azure Front Door with the Premium tier, and keep the mode at Detection.
On Managed rules, confirm that the Default rule set is assigned.
Add a custom rule of type Rate limit at priority 10 with a threshold of 100 requests per 1 minute, the condition RequestUri contains /login, and the action Block.
Add a custom geo-match rule that blocks one country you do not serve.
Associate the policy with a Front Door endpoint domain, send repeated requests to /login, and review the WAF logs.
Switch the policy mode to Prevention and repeat the test.
lab.verify: In Detection mode the logs show matched rules without blocking. In Prevention mode, excess /login requests from your IP are blocked until the next window and geo-blocked requests are blocked.

Add a per-rule exclusion for request header X-Session-Token on rule 942430
Add a custom rule with action Allow for all traffic
Disable the SQL injection rule group
questions.explanation: An exclusion skips only the named attribute for the scoped rule, which is the narrowest fix that Learn recommends. Detection mode stops all blocking. An Allow custom rule bypasses all managed rules for the matched traffic. Disabling the whole rule group removes SQL injection protection for every field.

questions.explanation: A Warning adds 3 to the anomaly score, below the threshold of 5, so it does not block on its own. Managed rules are supported only in Front Door Premium and Classic. objectives.summary: API Management protects back-end APIs by enforcing policies in the gateway: token validation (validate-jwt for any IdP, validate-azure-ad-token for Entra), throttling (rate-limit, rate-limit-by-key, quota, quota-by-key), caller IP filtering (ip-filter), mTLS validation (validate-client-certificate), and back-end authentication with the APIM managed identity (authentication-managed-identity). Tier availability and the difference between rate limits and quotas are frequent exam points.

keyFacts.fact: validate-jwt validates JWTs from any identity provider; validate-azure-ad-token is the specialized policy for tokens issued by Microsoft Entra. Both are available in all tiers.

rate-limit-by-key and quota-by-key use a custom key, such as an IP address or JWT subject, from a policy expression, and they are not available in the Consumption tier. Exceeding a limit returns 429 Too Many Requests.
Rate-limit counters are per gateway, so each region enforces them separately, while quota counters are global for the whole API Management instance.

ip-filter uses action allow or forbid with address or address-range elements and works in all tiers. With allow, requests that match no listed address are denied; with forbid, unmatched requests are allowed.

validate-client-certificate checks a client certificate against rules (trust, revocation, validity dates) and up to 10 identities (thumbprint, subject, issuer). Classic tiers need Negotiate client certificate, and Consumption and v2 tiers need Request client certificate.

authentication-managed-identity gets an Entra token for the resource attribute and sets it as a Bearer Authorization header. It uses the system-assigned identity unless client-id names a user-assigned one, and it caches the token until expiry.

objectives.portalPath: API Management > APIs > <API> > Design > Inbound processing > Policy code editor (</>)

lab.title: Protect an API with token validation, throttling and managed identity back-end auth
steps: Create an API Management instance in the Developer or Basic v2 tier and import a sample API.
Enable the system-assigned identity under Security > Managed identities.

In the API inbound policy, add <validate-azure-ad-token tenant-id="{{tenant}}"><client-application-ids><application-id>{{clientApp}}</application-id></client-application-ids></validate-azure-ad-token>
Add <rate-limit-by-key calls="10" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Request.IpAddress)" /> and <ip-filter action="allow"><address-range from="203.0.113.0" to="203.0.113.255" /></ip-filter>
Add <authentication-managed-identity resource="https://management.azure.com/" /> to call an ARM-backed endpoint.
Test from the Test tab and with curl, both with and without a valid token.
lab.verify: Calls without a token return 401, an 11th call within 60 seconds returns 429, calls from IPs outside the range return 403, and the back end receives a Bearer token.

objectives.summary: Defender for Cloud ships two posture plans. Foundational CSPM (free) gives asset inventory, MCSB recommendations, secure score, workflow automation and data export. Defender CSPM (paid) adds the cloud security graph and the features built on it: attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, agentless VM and container scanning, internet exposure analysis, DSPM, governance rules, critical asset protection, EASM integration and regulatory compliance assessments. Know which features need the paid plan and what is required to make them populate.

keyFacts.fact: Foundational CSPM (free) includes asset inventory, data export, workbooks, Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark recommendations, secure score, remediation tools and workflow automation. Attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, governance rules, agentless VM scanning and regulatory compliance assessments are not in Foundational CSPM; they come with Defender CSPM (agentless scanning is also in Servers Plan 2, and extra compliance standards can be unlocked by most other paid plans).
The cloud security graph is the context engine (assets, connections, exposure, permissions, vulnerabilities) that attack path analysis analyzes and that you query with cloud security explorer.

Attack paths start at an external, exploitable entry point, such as an internet-exposed vulnerable resource, and follow lateral movement to a critical target. Their remediation recommendations break the path.

Only the Subscription Owner can fully enable Defender CSPM. If someone with lower rights enables it, the agentless scanner stays off, and attack paths and security explorer do not populate with vulnerabilities.

The Defender CSPM components (agentless scanning for machines, agentless discovery for Kubernetes, container VA, sensitive data discovery, CIEM, serverless protection, serverless containers) are turned on individually under the plan Settings. Agentless Kubernetes discovery is required for attack path analysis.
Attack path and security explorer capabilities need either agentless VM scanning or the Defender for Servers vulnerability assessment capability to be enabled.

Deploy a small Linux VM with a public IP and SSH open to the internet.
After the scans run (up to 24 hours), open Cloud security explorer and pick a template such as internet-exposed VMs with high-severity vulnerabilities.
Open Attack path analysis and review any path that starts at the VM.

objectives.summary: The regulatory compliance dashboard maps Defender for Cloud assessments to controls in security standards that are implemented as Azure Policy initiatives. MCSB is assigned by default, and AWS and GCP connectors also get their own default benchmarks. Adding other standards such as PCI DSS, ISO 27001 or NIST needs a paid plan and the right RBAC permissions, and controls that cannot be assessed automatically appear greyed out.

keyFacts.fact: By default, Azure scopes get MCSB; AWS gets MCSB plus AWS Foundational Security Best Practices; GCP gets MCSB plus GCP Default.
Assigning standards requires onboarding any Defender plan except Defender for Servers Plan 1 or Defender for APIs Plan 1, plus Owner or Policy Contributor permissions.

To view the compliance data you need reader access to policy compliance data: the Reader role has it and Security Reader does not. Learn lists Resource Policy Contributor plus Security Admin as the minimum.

Defender for Servers has two plans with different scoping rules and features, which the exam tests heavily.

keyFacts.fact: Enable plans in Environment settings > <scope> > Defender plans; Enable all turns on every plan. Turning a plan off does not uninstall its extensions, which simply stop collecting data.

Defender for Storage, Defender for SQL and Defender for open-source relational databases can be enabled at the subscription or resource level. Defender for Servers and Defender for SQL servers on machines are also available at the workspace level.

Turning the Servers plan on defaults to Plan 2 (use Change plans to pick Plan 1). Plan 1 can be enabled or disabled per resource, but Plan 2 cannot be enabled at the resource level, only disabled there.

Enabling a Defender for Servers plan starts a 30-day trial that cannot be paused or extended, auto-provisions the Defender for Endpoint extension on supported machines, and enables Defender Vulnerability Management by default.
Use the built-in Azure Policy definition "Configure Azure Defender for Servers to be enabled" to enable plans at scale. To run both plans, split subscriptions into separate management groups.

objectives.summary: AWS accounts and GCP projects or organizations connect to Defender for Cloud through native, agentless security connectors created under Environment settings > Add environment. AWS uses a generated CloudFormation template (or Terraform) that creates IAM roles, with StackSets for management accounts. GCP uses a generated gcloud script that creates a workload identity pool, providers and service accounts for federated, keyless access. On-premises and other machines are connected through Azure Arc.

keyFacts.fact: Connecting AWS needs Contributor on the Azure subscription that hosts the connector. Enabling Defender CSPM on the connector needs subscription Owner, and CIEM needs Security Admin plus Application.ReadWrite.All.

AWS onboarding uses CloudFormation (an S3 URL or uploaded template) or Terraform, with Default or Least privilege access. A management account StackSet fails until trusted access for AWS Organizations is enabled.

GCP onboarding runs a generated gcloud script that creates a workload identity pool, a provider per plan, service accounts and project-level bindings. Defender exchanges Entra tokens with Google STS and impersonates the service account, so no long-lived keys are stored.
Organizations created after May 2024 enforce Domain Restricted Sharing by default, which can break the GCP script. Allow the Defender for Cloud principal set or customer ID in that policy.
Defender for Servers on AWS needs Azure Arc on EC2 instances (autoprovisioning needs Owner) and the AWS SSM Agent with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
When you create a GCP connector you choose a scan interval of 4, 6, 12 or 24 hours, although some data collectors use a fixed one-hour interval.

objectives.summary: Defender for Servers uses integrated Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management (MDVM) in two modes: agent-based scanning through the Defender for Endpoint sensor (Plan 1 or 2) and agentless disk-snapshot scanning (Plan 2 or Defender CSPM). Scanning is on by default and can be adjusted under the Servers plan settings. Premium MDVM features are Plan 2 only, and BYOL Qualys or Rapid7 is an alternative.

keyFacts.fact: Agent-based vulnerability scanning uses the Defender for Endpoint integration and is available in Servers Plan 1 and Plan 2. Agentless vulnerability scanning in Defender for Servers is Plan 2 only.
Agentless machine scanning is on by default with Servers Plan 2 or Defender CSPM. It uses disk snapshots, needs no agent or network connectivity and does not affect machine performance.

Scanning is on by default once Defender for Servers is enabled. To set it manually: Environment settings > <subscription> > Defender for Servers plan > Monitoring coverage > Settings, turn on Vulnerability assessment for machines, then pick the solution under Edit configuration.
Deploying the scanner requires Owner at the resource group level, and viewing findings requires Security Reader.

Premium MDVM capabilities, such as security baselines assessment, blocking vulnerable applications, browser extension, certificate, network share and hardware or firmware assessment, need Servers Plan 2. Plan 1 includes vulnerability, configuration and software inventory assessment.
BYOL scanners (Qualys, Rapid7) report to the partner platform and back into Defender for Cloud, and they do not need a paid Defender plan.

objectives.summary: Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management (Defender EASM) discovers your internet-facing assets from the outside in. It starts from seeds (domains, IP blocks, hosts, email contacts, ASNs, Whois organizations), labels the discovered assets with inventory states, and surfaces observations such as CVEs. Defender CSPM includes EASM integration at no extra license for outside-in exposure data. A standalone Defender EASM resource gives full discovery groups and inventory, with billing only for Approved Inventory assets after a 30-day trial.

keyFacts.fact: EASM integration is included with Defender CSPM by default and needs no Defender EASM license. It powers outside-in discovery of internet-facing resources, attack paths starting from exposed IPs, and security explorer queries.

Discovery seeds can be organization names, domains, IP blocks, hosts, email contacts, ASNs and Whois organizations. Private IP addresses cannot be seeds, and you can add exclusions such as unrelated subsidiaries.

Asset states are Approved Inventory, Dependency, Monitor Only, Candidate and Requires Investigation. Approved Inventory assets are scanned daily and shown in dashboards, while Candidates are scanned only during discovery and need manual review.
A new Defender EASM resource has a 30-day free trial. After that, only Approved Inventory host:IP combinations, domains and IP addresses are billable, and duplicate hosts are not counted.

Discovery groups run on their own recurrence, Weekly by default and recommended; choose Never for a one-time run. You can also start from a prebuilt attack surface with Getting Started > Build my Attack Surface.

objectives.portalPath: Defender EASM resource > Manage > Discovery > Add Discovery Group; Defender EASM resource > General > Getting Started; Inventory

lab.title: Create a Defender EASM resource and run a discovery group
steps: In the Azure portal, create a Microsoft Defender EASM resource in a lab resource group. The 30-day trial starts.
Open Getting Started, search for your organization in the prebuilt attack surfaces, and if none matches, continue to a custom discovery.
Go to Manage > Discovery > Add Discovery Group, enter a name and keep Recurring Frequency at Weekly.
Add seeds such as a domain you own and its public IP block, and add an exclusion for any subsidiary domain.
Select Review + Create, then Create & Run.
When the run completes, open Inventory, filter by Candidate, and move confirmed assets to Approved Inventory.
lab.verify: The Inventory shows assets under Approved Inventory and Candidate, and the dashboards update with observations for approved assets.

objectives.summary: Microsoft Sentinel runs on top of a Log Analytics workspace: you create (or pick) a workspace, add Sentinel to it, then connect it to the Microsoft Defender portal for unified security operations. The Defender portal uses one primary workspace (which receives Defender XDR incidents/alerts) plus any number of secondary workspaces. Onboarding to the Sentinel data lake is a separate, one-time, tenant-level step that requires the workspace to be connected as primary. Sentinel in the Azure portal is being retired, so new deployments should be planned around the Defender portal.

keyFacts.fact: Enabling Microsoft Sentinel requires Contributor on the subscription that holds the workspace; default workspaces created by Defender for Cloud can't host Sentinel, and a Sentinel workspace can't later be moved to another resource group or subscription.
New customers who hold subscription Owner or User Access Administrator are automatically onboarded to the Defender portal and use Sentinel there only.

The Defender portal supports one primary and unlimited secondary Sentinel workspaces per tenant; the Defender XDR incidents/alerts connector attaches only to the primary, and switching primary moves that connector automatically.

Onboarding a workspace to the Defender portal requires an unconditional Owner assignment at subscription scope (or User Access Administrator plus Sentinel Contributor); with more than one Sentinel workspace you also need at least Security Administrator in Entra ID.

Data lake onboarding is a one-time tenant setup (up to about 60 minutes) started from System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > Data lake; the lake lives in the primary workspace's region, and only same-region connected workspaces are attached. Entra Security Administrator or Global Administrator is required.
After March 31, 2027, Sentinel is supported only in the Defender portal; Workspace Manager isn't available there, so use repositories (preview) or multitenant management to distribute content.

Sign in to https://security.microsoft.com, go to System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > SIEM workspaces.
Select LAW-Contoso-SOC > Connect workspace and set it as Primary; read the product-change notice and confirm.

(Optional, if you have Security Administrator) Go to System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > Data lake > Start setup, choose the subscription and resource group for billing, then select Set up data lake.

objectives.summary: Sentinel SIEM access uses Azure RBAC built-in roles (Reader, Responder, Contributor, Playbook Operator, Automation Contributor), ideally assigned at the resource group that holds the workspace. Playbooks are Logic Apps, so creating/editing them needs Logic App Contributor, and the Sentinel service account needs Automation Contributor on the playbook resource group before automation rules can run them. Data lake access is governed by Microsoft Entra ID roles or Defender unified RBAC.

keyFacts.fact: Reader views data, incidents and workbooks; Responder adds incident management; Contributor adds installing/updating solutions and creating/editing resources such as analytics rules.
Playbook Operator lets a user list, view and manually run playbooks; Logic App Contributor is needed to create or edit playbooks.

Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor is assigned to the Sentinel service account (not users) on the playbook resource group so automation rules can run playbooks; granting it requires Owner or User Access Administrator.

Microsoft recommends assigning Sentinel roles at the resource group containing the workspace; if you assign at the workspace instead, you must also assign them on the SecurityInsights solution resource.
Creating or deleting workbooks needs Workbook Contributor in addition to a Sentinel role; guest users who assign incidents need Directory Reader plus Responder.
Playbook Operator, Automation Contributor and Workbook Contributor aren't available in Defender unified RBAC and must still be managed in the Azure portal.

objectives.summary: The Syslog via AMA and CEF via AMA connectors install the Azure Monitor Agent on a Linux machine (the source itself or a dedicated log forwarder) and push a data collection rule (DCR) that selects facilities and minimum severities. Plain syslog lands in the Syslog table and CEF in CommonSecurityLog. A forwarder also needs the installation script, which configures rsyslog/syslog-ng to listen on port 514.

keyFacts.fact: CEF messages land in CommonSecurityLog and Syslog messages in Syslog; AMA supports RFC 3164 and RFC 5424 syslog formats.
Selecting a log level in the portal DCR collects that level and everything more severe (for example LOG_ERR also collects CRIT, ALERT, EMERG); the API lets you filter specific levels.
Using the same facility for Syslog and CEF can duplicate data between Syslog and CommonSecurityLog; separate facilities or add an ingestion-time transformation to filter CEF out of the Syslog stream.
The forwarder installation script configures rsyslog or syslog-ng and opens port 514 (TCP and UDP); AMA 1.28.11+ receives from the daemon on TCP 28330.
Non-Azure forwarders need Azure Arc (Connected Machine agent) installed to appear in the DCR resource list.
AMA-based data connectors need an internet connection from the agent machine; allow outbound port 443 to Microsoft Sentinel.
In the API DCR, the stream is Microsoft-Syslog for syslog and Microsoft-CommonSecurityLog for CEF.

objectives.summary: The Windows Security Events via AMA connector uses a DCR to collect Security/AppLocker events into SecurityEvent, using predefined sets (All, Common, Minimal) or Custom XPath queries. Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) centralizes events on a Windows Event Collector (WEC); the Windows Forwarded Events connector, with AMA on the WEC, writes them to WindowsEvent instead. Many built-in analytics rules query SecurityEvent, so table choice matters.

keyFacts.fact: All = full Security and AppLocker logs (not Application/System); Common = full user audit trail (includes 4624 and 4634); Minimal = breach-indicating events only (includes 4624/4625/4688 but not 4634); Custom = XPath in the DCR.
Windows Security Events via AMA writes to SecurityEvent; Windows Forwarded Events writes to WindowsEvent, even for forwarded Security log events.
The Windows Forwarded Events connector requires WEC enabled and running with AMA installed on the WEC machine; Microsoft recommends deploying the ASIM WindowsEvent parsers.
AMA supports XPath 1.0 only; test a query with Get-WinEvent -FilterXPath before using it in a DCR.
Non-Azure Windows servers must have Azure Arc installed and enabled before you enable an AMA-based connector.
Selecting the Security log in a generic Azure Monitor DCR sends events to the Event table, whereas the Sentinel connector sends the same events to SecurityEvent.

objectives.summary: Custom tables store data that has no built-in table. Their names end in _CL and they are fed through DCRs: either text-file collection with AMA (Custom Logs via AMA) or the Logs Ingestion API, where an app sends JSON to a DCR endpoint or DCE. The DCR declares the input stream and an optional KQL transformation that shapes the data to the table schema.

keyFacts.fact: Custom tables used with the Logs Ingestion API must have the _CL suffix; the portal adds it automatically when you create a 'New custom log (DCR-based)'.
The Logs Ingestion API needs an app registration (or managed identity), the target table, a DCR, and the Monitoring Metrics Publisher role on the DCR for the sending identity.
Role assignments on a DCR can take up to 30 minutes to propagate; sending earlier returns HTTP 403.
A Direct-kind DCR provides its own logsIngestion endpoint, so a separate DCE isn't required unless you use private link.
For Custom Logs via AMA, the destination _CL table should contain TimeGenerated (datetime) and RawData (string), or Message when collecting from a forwarder.
Custom columns added to an Azure (built-in) table must use the _CF suffix; certain names such as TenantId, Type and _ResourceId are reserved.

Run: az extension add --name monitor-control-service, then az monitor data-collection rule create --resource-group RG-SOC --name DCR-AppAudit --rule-file ./my-dcr.json
Register an app in Entra ID and assign it Monitoring Metrics Publisher on DCR-AppAudit (Access control (IAM)).

objectives.summary: Automation rules are lightweight, centrally managed rules triggered when an incident is created or updated or an alert is created; they can assign owners, change status/severity, add tags or tasks, and run playbooks, in a defined order. Playbooks are Azure Logic Apps workflows for complex or external actions (for example, isolating a device or creating a ticket). Calling playbooks directly from analytics rules is deprecated, so automation rules are the way to trigger them.

keyFacts.fact: Automation rule triggers are incident created, incident updated, and alert created; for the alert trigger, the only available action is Run playbook.
Only incident-trigger playbooks can run from incident-trigger rules and only alert-trigger playbooks from alert-trigger rules; both Standard and Consumption logic apps are supported.
Rules run sequentially by Order number and actions run in listed order; later rules see the incident as changed by earlier ones, and update-trigger rules have their own queue.
Rules can have an expiration date, useful for suppressing noise during a time-boxed penetration test.

Adding playbooks directly to analytics rules has been blocked since June 2023, and that legacy method was deprecated as of March 2026; invoke playbooks from automation rules (alert-created trigger) instead.
Changes made by automation rules can be audited with SecurityIncident | where ModifiedBy contains "Automation".

objectives.summary: Retention in Sentinel combines the Analytics tier (hot, interactive 'analytics retention') with total retention mirrored into the Sentinel data lake for up to 12 years, or ingesting directly to the Data Lake tier for cheap, lower-performance storage. In Azure Monitor terms, tables use the Analytics, Basic or Auxiliary/Lake plan, and long-term retention extends data beyond the interactive window. Settings are per table and managed in the Defender portal Tables page or the Log Analytics Tables blade.

keyFacts.fact: Analytics retention for Sentinel workspaces defaults to 90 days and can be extended to two years (730 days) at a prorated long-term retention charge; total retention can reach 12 years.
Defender XDR advanced hunting data stays in the XDR default tier for 30 days; extending supported XDR tables up to 90 days incurs Sentinel ingestion but no extra storage cost.

Data Lake tier: minimal ingestion cost and slower queries; analytics rules, hunting queries, watchlists, workbooks and playbooks are limited, and Restore and data export aren't available (KQL/notebook jobs can promote data to the analytics tier).
Switching a table from Analytics to Data Lake stops real-time analytics and hunting queries on it; shortening total retention waits 30 days before deleting data.

Basic tables are queryable for 30 days (queries billed per GB scanned); Auxiliary tables are queryable for the whole retention period with unoptimized performance; switching to Auxiliary stops alerts on that table.
A table's plan can be changed only once per week; total retention up to 4,383 days (12 years) can be set per table.

objectives.summary: Microsoft Purview Audit (the unified audit log) records user and admin activity across Microsoft 365. In the Defender portal you can run the same audit search as in Purview (Audit page), and hunt over Microsoft 365 audit events with KQL in advanced hunting through the CloudAppEvents table, which Defender for Cloud Apps populates when the Microsoft 365 app connector is enabled with Microsoft 365 activities. Purview DLP and insider risk data also surface in advanced hunting tables such as CloudAppEvents and DataSecurityEvents (preview).

keyFacts.fact: CloudAppEvents holds events for accounts and objects in Office 365 and other connected cloud apps; it's populated only if Defender for Cloud Apps is connected to Microsoft 365 with 'Microsoft 365 activities' selected.
To monitor Microsoft 365 activities in Defender for Cloud Apps, auditing must be enabled in Microsoft Purview.
The Defender portal Audit page (security.microsoft.com/auditlogsearch) provides the Purview audit search; access needs the View-Only Audit Logs or Audit Logs role.

Audit (Standard) keeps records 180 days (90 days for logs before Oct 17, 2023); Audit (Premium) keeps Entra, Exchange, OneDrive and SharePoint records one year by default, with retention policies up to 10 years with an add-on.
Advanced hunting explores up to 30 days of raw Defender XDR data, plus analytics-tier data per workspace retention when Sentinel is onboarded.
DLP 'Go hunt' built-in queries (preview) use CloudAppEvents, which contains Purview DLP audit data across SharePoint, OneDrive, Exchange and devices.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender portal > Investigation & response > Hunting > Advanced hunting (CloudAppEvents); Microsoft Defender portal > Audit

lab.title: Hunt Microsoft 365 file downloads in CloudAppEvents
steps: Confirm auditing is on: in Exchange Online PowerShell run Get-AdminAuditLogConfig | Format-List UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled and expect True. Don't use Security & Compliance PowerShell for this check; there the value always shows False (see https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/audit-log-enable-disable).
In the Defender portal open Settings > Cloud apps > App connectors > Connect an app > Microsoft 365, keep all components (including Microsoft 365 activities) selected and connect.
Download a file from a SharePoint site as a test user.
In Hunting > Advanced hunting run: CloudAppEvents | where ActionType == "FileDownloaded" | project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, Application, ObjectName, IPAddress | take 50
lab.verify: The query returns the test download; the same activity also appears in an Audit search on the Defender portal Audit page.

objectives.summary: A Security Copilot workspace is a tenant-bound container that sets where customer data is stored, which SCU capacity powers it, and who has access (owners and contributors are scoped per workspace). Organizations can create several workspaces to separate teams, regions or budgets. Capacity is measured in Security Compute Units (SCUs): provisioned SCUs are billed hourly, and optional overage SCUs absorb spikes. Microsoft 365 E5/E7 tenants can be auto-provisioned with a default workspace and capacity. Workspaces were introduced in public preview, while workspace-level plugin management is GA.

keyFacts.fact: A workspace defines the customer data storage location, the capacity that powers it, and who has access; owners/contributors are scoped per workspace.
Creating a workspace requires at least Security Administrator; attaching capacity also requires Azure subscription Owner or Contributor.
A workspace's data storage location is chosen at creation and can't be changed afterward.
Provisioned capacity requires a minimum of one SCU, refreshes each clock hour, and unused SCUs don't roll over; overage SCUs are billed on use (to one decimal) and can be capped or unlimited.
Owner settings apply per workspace, except audit logging enablement, which only Security Admins can change and which applies to all workspaces.

For eligible Microsoft 365 E5/E7 tenants, Security Copilot auto-creates a default virtual capacity and default workspace; embedded experiences in Defender, Entra, Purview and Intune use the default workspace.
Security Copilot workspaces were introduced in public preview; managing plugins at workspace level is generally available. Check the current status before your exam.

objectives.portalPath: Security Copilot portal (securitycopilot.microsoft.com) > workspace selector > New workspace; Home menu > Owner settings > Manage workspaces

lab.title: Create a second workspace with its own capacity
steps: Sign in to https://securitycopilot.microsoft.com as a Security Administrator who is also Contributor on an Azure subscription.
Open the workspace selector on the landing page and select New workspace.

Name it WS-Contoso-EU, create a new capacity (subscription, resource group, capacity name, prompt evaluation location, 1 SCU, overage limit), select the data storage location and data sharing preferences.
Accept the terms and select Create; then open Owner settings > Manage workspaces and confirm the capacity assignment.
Delete the capacity when finished to stop hourly billing (Owner settings > units > Change > ... > Delete the capacity).
lab.verify: WS-Contoso-EU appears in the workspace selector and in Manage workspaces with its capacity; Usage monitoring shows the capacity.

objectives.summary: Security Copilot has two platform roles, Copilot owner and Copilot contributor, which control platform features but grant no security data by themselves. Certain Entra and Purview roles (for example Global Administrator and Security Administrator) automatically inherit owner. Access to data still depends on each plugin's own RBAC, because Copilot uses on-behalf-of authentication. Best practice is to replace broad 'Everyone' contributor access with the Recommended Microsoft Security roles group or specific security groups.

keyFacts.fact: Copilot owner and Copilot contributor aren't Entra roles; they control only Security Copilot platform capabilities and give no access to security data by themselves.

Billing Administrator, Entra Compliance Administrator, Global Administrator, Intune Administrator and Security Administrator, plus some Purview roles, automatically inherit Copilot owner; Security Copilot enforces at least two owners.
Only owners can manage capacity, view the usage dashboard, change preinstalled plugin availability, and update data sharing options; contributors can create sessions and run/share promptbooks.
Plugins use on-behalf-of authentication, so an analyst with Copilot contributor still needs, for example, Microsoft Sentinel Reader to see Sentinel incidents through Copilot.
Use the Recommended Microsoft Security roles group (default) instead of Everyone; if Everyone is assigned, remove it first.
For MSSPs, GDAP is recommended and uses the customer's capacity; Azure Lighthouse uses the partner tenant's capacity.

Assign Analyst1 Microsoft Sentinel Reader on the Sentinel resource group so the Sentinel plugin returns data.
lab.verify: Analyst1 can open a session and ask about a Sentinel incident; a user outside the group can no longer access the platform.

objectives.summary: Plugins give Security Copilot tools to reach data and services. Categories are Microsoft, non-Microsoft, websites and custom. Owners control whether contributors can add custom plugins for themselves or for everyone in the workspace, and can restrict preinstalled plugins to owners only. Custom plugins are YAML/JSON manifests (Descriptor and SkillGroups) using formats such as API (OpenAPI 3.0/3.0.1), KQL, GPT, or an OpenAI plugin link.

keyFacts.fact: Plugin sources are grouped as Microsoft, Non-Microsoft, Websites and Custom; users toggle plugins on or off in the Sources pane.
By default only owners can add custom plugins; owners can allow 'Owners and Contributors' for user scope and separately for organization/workspace scope.
Restricting a preinstalled plugin to Owners only takes effect immediately and affects embedded experiences too; new preinstalled plugins then default to owners only.
Plugins such as Microsoft Sentinel need per-user setup (gear/Set up), for example to choose a default workspace.
A custom plugin manifest has two required top-level keys, Descriptor and SkillGroups; API plugins support OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.0.1.
Products that integrate as plugins (such as non-Microsoft services) must be purchased separately.

objectives.portalPath: Security Copilot portal > prompt bar > Sources icon > Manage plugins; Home menu > Owner settings > Plugin settings

lab.title: Allow contributors to add personal custom plugins and upload a KQL plugin
steps: As an owner, open Owner settings > Plugin settings and set 'Who can add and manage their own custom plugins' to Owners and Contributors.

Create a YAML file with Descriptor (Name, DisplayName, Description, Settings for TenantId, WorkspaceName, SubscriptionId, ResourceGroupName) and a SkillGroups entry with Format: KQL, Target: Sentinel and a simple query such as SecurityIncident | take 10.
Select the Sources icon > Custom > Upload plugin, choose 'Just me', Security Copilot plugin, upload the file.
Complete the plugin setup values, then turn on the plugin toggle.
lab.verify: The plugin appears in the Custom section with a private tag and its skill can be invoked from the prompt bar.

objectives.summary: Security Copilot agents automate tasks such as phishing triage, threat intelligence briefings and Conditional Access optimization. You discover them in the Agents library or the Microsoft Security Store, set them up with an identity (a dedicated Microsoft Entra Agent ID is recommended), trigger and permissions, and then run, pause, edit and tune them through feedback and memory. Partner agents are bought in Security Store; agents that access Microsoft product data need Global Administrator approval. The agent and Security Store Learn pages carry a prerelease notice, and expanding the Phishing Triage Agent to other alert types is in preview.

keyFacts.fact: Agent setup lets you create an agent identity (Microsoft Entra Agent ID, currently Microsoft-built agents only) or connect an existing user account; creating an agent identity is recommended.

A partner-built agent that accesses Microsoft product data (for example Intune, Entra, Sentinel, Defender) requires a Global Administrator to approve its permissions before owners/contributors finish setup.
Security Store purchases are separate from Security Copilot: removing an agent doesn't end its subscription, and running agents consumes SCUs billed independently.
Getting an agent from Security Store needs Contributor or Owner on the Azure billing subscription and a Security Copilot owner or contributor role to set it up.

The Phishing Triage Agent needs Security Copilot capacity, Defender for Office 365 Plan 2, URBAC activated for Defender for Office 365, and the 'Email reported by user as malware or phish' alert policy; it auto-activates its plugins.
Feedback given to an agent is stored in its memory; owners/contributors can review it via Manage memory and reject feedback.

lab.title: Set up a Microsoft-built agent with an Agent ID

Choose a Microsoft-built agent available in your tenant (for example Threat Intelligence Briefing Agent) and select Set up.
Choose Create an agent identity, review required permissions, plugins and products, and set the trigger (scheduled or manual).
Complete setup, then select Run > One time.
After the run, give feedback to the agent and review it under ... > Manage memory.
lab.verify: The agent shows in Active agents / Agents in use with run history and output, and your feedback appears in Manage memory.
